Carbapenems are time-dependent with a target of about 40% fT>MIC. At an MIC of 2 mcg/mL, the CLSI susceptible breakpoint for P. aeruginosa, 30-minute infusions may miss the target, and a 3-hour infusion prolongs time above MIC and raises the probability of target attainment.
AUC0-24/MIC of 125 or more is a fluoroquinolone target; it is not the primary pharmacodynamic index for meropenem or other beta-lactams.

q: An intubated patient on fentanyl infusion at 100 mcg/hr develops acute-onset hyperthermia (40.1°C), agitation, diaphoresis, and myoclonus 4 hours after starting linezolid for VRE pneumonia. Fentanyl was started 2 days earlier. Which mechanism best explains this presentation?
opts: A. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia from high-dose fentanyl
B. Serotonin syndrome: fentanyl (weak serotonergic) + linezolid (MAO-A inhibitor) → excess serotonin
C. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from dopamine receptor blockade
D. Anticholinergic toxidrome from atropine pretreatment
exp: Linezolid is a weak, reversible MAO-A and MAO-B inhibitor. Fentanyl has weak serotonin reuptake inhibition properties (like many synthetic opioids — meperidine being the strongest). Combined, they can precipitate SEROTONIN SYNDROME: triad of hyperthermia, neuromuscular excitability (myoclonus, clonus, hyperreflexia), and autonomic instability (diaphoresis, tachycardia). Onset within hours of adding the second serotonergic agent. Management: discontinue all serotonergic drugs, cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) orally if tolerates, supportive care, benzodiazepines for agitation/rigidity. NMS: slower onset (days–weeks), associated with antipsychotics (dopamine blockers), lead-pipe rigidity (not myoclonus), no hyperreflexia. Opioid hyperalgesia lacks hyperthermia and myoclonus.
ref: Vol 1 ID (linezolid toxicity); Vol 2 Neurology; ISMP Linezolid Interactions
opts_exp: A. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia presents as paradoxical pain hypersensitivity with chronic opioid use — NOT acute hyperthermia and myoclonus after adding a new drug. No autonomic instability.

B. CORRECT. Linezolid (MAO-A inhibitor) + fentanyl (weak serotonergic effect) = serotonin syndrome. Classic triad: altered mental status, autonomic instability, neuromuscular findings (myoclonus, hyperreflexia, clonus). Onset within hours. Hunter Criteria positive: clonus/myoclonus + MAO inhibitor within 24 hrs = serotonin syndrome confirmed.

C. NMS requires a dopamine-blocking agent (antipsychotics, metoclopramide). Onset is days to weeks. Features: 'lead-pipe' rigidity (not myoclonus), hyperthermia, autonomic instability, elevated CK. No myoclonus. Linezolid is not a dopamine blocker.

D. Anticholinergic toxidrome: dry skin (not diaphoresis), urinary retention, decreased bowel sounds, tachycardia, mydriasis. Diaphoresis RULES OUT anticholinergic toxidrome — skin is dry in anticholinergic.

q: A post-cardiac surgery patient on venoarterial ECMO develops methicillin-resistant S. aureus bacteremia. Despite vancomycin 1500 mg IV q12h, the Bayesian-estimated AUC24 is 300 mg·h/L (target 400-600, assuming MIC 1 mg/L), and renal function is stable. The ECMO circuit has been running for 48 hours. What best explains the subtherapeutic exposure, and what is the best corrective action?
opts: A. Increased hepatic first-pass metabolism due to ECMO-induced hepatic blood flow redirection

B. An expanded volume of distribution (circuit priming volume, hemodilution, capillary leak, and to a lesser extent circuit adsorption) — give a supplemental loading dose, increase the maintenance dose, and titrate with AUC-guided monitoring
C. ECMO-induced hemolysis releases free hemoglobin that binds and inactivates vancomycin
D. The patient needs peritoneal dialysis to remove ECMO-related metabolites competing for vancomycin binding
exp: ECMO can change drug PK by adding circuit priming volume and causing hemodilution. It is also used in critically ill patients with capillary leak and fluid overload, so the volume of distribution expands and drug exposure falls. Circuit sequestration mainly affects lipophilic, highly protein-bound drugs (fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, voriconazole). Vancomycin is hydrophilic with low-to-moderate protein binding, so circuit adsorption is minimal, and the Vd effect is driven mainly by priming and fluid shifts. Management per the 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP vancomycin consensus: give a loading dose (20-35 mg/kg actual body weight in critical illness), increase the maintenance dose, and use Bayesian AUC-guided monitoring with a target AUC24 of 400-600 mg·h/L (trough-only targeting of 15-20 mcg/mL is no longer recommended for serious MRSA infection). A is wrong: IV vancomycin has no first-pass metabolism and is not hepatically cleared. C is wrong: free hemoglobin does not inactivate vancomycin. D is wrong: dialysis would remove vancomycin, and no such competing metabolites exist.
ref: Vol 2 Pharmacokinetics; SCCM ECMO Pharmacokinetics Review
opts_exp: IV vancomycin has no first-pass metabolism and is not hepatically cleared, so changes in hepatic blood flow do not explain the low AUC.

ECMO priming volume, hemodilution, capillary leak, and fluid overload expand vancomycin's volume of distribution; because vancomycin is hydrophilic with low-to-moderate protein binding, circuit adsorption plays only a minor role. Per the 2020 vancomycin consensus guideline, give a loading dose (20-35 mg/kg actual body weight), increase the maintenance dose, and titrate with Bayesian AUC monitoring to 400-600 mg·h/L.
Free hemoglobin released by hemolysis does not bind or inactivate vancomycin; this is not a recognized mechanism.
No ECMO-related metabolites compete for vancomycin binding, and dialysis would remove vancomycin and lower exposure further.

q: An adult is prescribed gentamicin 7 mg/kg using a validated Hartford extended-interval protocol. Which monitoring approach matches the nomogram’s intended use?
opts: A. Plot an appropriately timed 6–14-hour concentration to select an interval according to the protocol
B. Apply the nomogram unchanged to any aminoglycoside dose
C. Use it automatically in every pregnant or dialysis patient
D. Reduce every dose to 5 mg/kg without consulting the protocol
exp: The Hartford approach uses a timed concentration after the specified high dose to select a dosing interval. Dose, sample timing, renal function, eligible population, and the exact local protocol must be checked; do not memorize or invent graph boundaries.
ref: Vol 2 Pharmacokinetics; Hartford Nomogram (Nicolau et al.)
opts_exp: A. Correct. Plot the actual elapsed time and concentration on the validated protocol nomogram.
B. The nomogram assumes a specified dose; concentrations from other regimens cannot simply be interpreted unchanged.
C. Extended-interval protocols have population exclusions and renal-function limitations; pregnancy and dialysis need specific assessment.
D. Changing the dose invalidates the original nomogram assumptions unless the protocol explicitly supports the adjustment.
reviewNote: Targeted correction 2026-10-19; full chapter review pending.

q: A pharmacist is performing a prospective drug use evaluation of heparin infusions. A frail 78-year-old woman (5'2", 48 kg; normal hepatic function) admitted for NSTEMI is started on weight-based IV heparin; she also received heparin during a cardiac catheterization 3 weeks ago. Her anti-Xa level 6 hours after the bolus is 0.6 IU/mL (target 0.3-0.7). Six hours later (about 12 hours into therapy), her platelet count falls from 220,000 to 88,000/mm3. 4T score: thrombocytopenia 2, timing 2 (fall within 1 day with heparin exposure in the past 30 days), thrombosis 1, other causes 0. What is the correct immediate management?
opts: A. Discontinue heparin, start warfarin immediately at 10 mg/day
B. Discontinue all heparin, start argatroban 2 mcg/kg/min (titrated to aPTT 1.5-3 times baseline), and avoid warfarin until the platelet count recovers to ≥150,000/mm3
C. Switch to enoxaparin (LMWH), because cross-reactivity with HIT antibodies is rare
D. Reduce heparin dose by 50% and recheck platelet count in 24 hours
exp: The 4T score is 2 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 5, which is intermediate probability (0-3 low, 4-5 intermediate, 6-8 high). A rapid-onset fall within 24 hours scores 2 timing points only because she was exposed to heparin within the past 30 days. ASH 2018: for intermediate or high probability, stop all heparin (including flushes and heparin-coated catheters), start a therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, danaparoid, or a DOAC), and send a PF4/heparin immunoassay. Argatroban is hepatically cleared; the labeled starting dose is 2 mcg/kg/min, reduced (for example, 0.5 mcg/kg/min) in hepatic impairment, and lower starting doses are often used in critical illness or heart failure. Titrate to an aPTT of 1.5-3 times baseline. A is wrong: warfarin started in acute HIT depletes protein C and can cause venous limb gangrene; start it only after platelet recovery (≥150,000/mm3) with at least 5 days of overlap. C is wrong: enoxaparin cross-reacts extensively with HIT antibodies (fondaparinux, a synthetic pentasaccharide, rarely cross-reacts and is not an LMWH). D is wrong: any continued heparin exposure fuels thrombosis.
opts_exp: Warfarin started in acute HIT depletes protein C before thrombin generation falls and can cause venous limb gangrene, and a 10 mg dose makes this more likely. Start warfarin only after platelets recover to at least 150,000/mm3, with at least 5 days of overlap.

Her 4T score is 2 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 5, an intermediate probability, so ASH 2018 calls for stopping all heparin, starting a therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulant, and sending a PF4/heparin immunoassay. With normal hepatic function, argatroban at the labeled 2 mcg/kg/min titrated to an aPTT of 1.5-3 times baseline is appropriate, and warfarin waits until platelets reach at least 150,000/mm3.
Enoxaparin cross-reacts extensively with HIT antibodies; the rare cross-reactivity applies to fondaparinux, a synthetic pentasaccharide that is not an LMWH.
Any continued heparin exposure, even at a reduced dose, keeps generating HIT antibody complexes and fuels thrombosis, and waiting 24 hours delays needed anticoagulation.

q: A meta-analysis of 8 RCTs comparing Drug A vs. placebo for acute MI mortality reports RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.61–0.99, p=0.04) with I² = 72%. One large RCT (n=6,400) contributes 60% of the total weight. A funnel plot shows asymmetry with small studies plotting mostly on one side. Which is the most appropriate conclusion about the evidence?
opts: A. Drug A significantly reduces MI mortality; strong evidence supports routine use

B. The meta-analysis shows significant heterogeneity (I²=72%) and possible publication bias; the pooled estimate should be interpreted cautiously, and the single dominant trial should be evaluated independently
C. I² of 72% invalidates the meta-analysis entirely; no conclusions can be drawn
D. Funnel plot asymmetry proves publication bias; Drug A has no mortality benefit
exp: Critical appraisal of meta-analysis: I² = 72% indicates HIGH statistical heterogeneity (thresholds: <25% low, 25–50% moderate, >50% high). High I² means individual trials differ substantially in effect — pooling may be inappropriate or misleading. Funnel plot asymmetry SUGGESTS (but does not prove) publication bias — small studies showing negative results may be unpublished (Egger's test required). When one trial dominates (60% weight), the meta-analysis result is largely driven by that single study; independent critical appraisal of the dominant RCT is crucial. The correct interpretation: statistically significant but HIGH uncertainty due to heterogeneity and potential publication bias — interpret cautiously. I² alone doesn't invalidate a meta-analysis (heterogeneity may be explicable by subgroup analysis). Funnel plot asymmetry has multiple explanations beyond publication bias (clinical heterogeneity, methodologic variation).
ref: Vol 2 Drug Information/Biostatistics; Cochrane Handbook Chapter 9
opts_exp: A. 'Strong evidence supports routine use' is an overstatement. I²=72% means the 8 trials have heterogeneous results — the pooled RR may not represent any individual population well. Borderline p-value (0.04) combined with high heterogeneity should prompt caution.

B. CORRECT. Proper critical appraisal: acknowledge significant heterogeneity (I²=72%), funnel plot asymmetry raising publication bias concern, and dominant-trial effect. Evaluate the 6,400-patient RCT independently to see if it alone crosses significance. Pooled estimate is statistically significant but should be viewed with uncertainty pending explanation of heterogeneity.

C. High I² does not invalidate a meta-analysis — it indicates heterogeneity that requires explanation (subgroup analysis, meta-regression). Concluding no conclusions can be drawn is overly nihilistic.

D. Funnel plot asymmetry is suggestive but not proof of publication bias. Other causes: small-study effects, clinical heterogeneity, language bias. It does not allow conclusion that Drug A 'has no benefit.'

q: A clinical pharmacist calculates an NNT of 25 for Drug B in preventing 30-day cardiovascular death (ARR = 4%). The drug costs $8,000/year and adds one year of therapy per patient treated. During budget impact analysis, what is the cost per event prevented (not cost-effectiveness — just direct acquisition cost calculation)?
opts: A. $8,000 (one patient's annual drug cost)
B. $200,000 (NNT × annual drug cost per patient)
C. $32,000 (NNT × monthly drug cost)
D. $320 (drug cost divided by ARR percentage)
exp: Cost per event prevented = NNT × cost per patient treated. NNT = 25 means 25 patients must receive the drug for 1 year to prevent one event. Cost per patient = $8,000/year. Cost per event prevented = 25 × $8,000 = $200,000. This is a budget impact metric (NOT ICER — which would divide by QALY gained). ICER (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio) = incremental cost ÷ incremental effectiveness (QALYs). A threshold of $50,000–$150,000 per QALY is often used (NICE: £20,000–£30,000/QALY). Cost per event prevented = $200,000. Whether this is cost-effective depends on the severity of the prevented event and QALY framework.
opts_exp: A. $8,000 is the cost for one patient — does not account for NNT. You must treat 25 patients to prevent 1 event.
B. CORRECT. Cost per event prevented = NNT × cost per patient = 25 × $8,000 = $200,000. This represents the total acquisition cost required to achieve one event prevented in the population.

C. Monthly cost: $8,000/12 = $667/month. $667 × 25 × 12 months = $200,000 — this is just NNT × annual cost expressed via monthly calculation. $32,000 would be NNT × monthly cost ($1,280/month × 25) but that's wrong math: $8,000/12 × 25 = ~$16,667. $32,000 is mathematically incorrect.
D. $320 = $8,000/25 — this divides rather than multiplies. No pharmacoeconomic metric uses this calculation.

q: A patient has persistent H. pylori infection after first-line clarithromycin-based triple therapy (omeprazole 20 mg BID). Genotyping shows CYP2C19 *17/*17 (ultrarapid metabolizer). Which management best accounts for the pharmacogenomic findings?
opts: A. Use omeprazole at standard dose 20 mg BID — the issue is clarithromycin resistance, not PPI metabolism
B. In a salvage regimen that avoids repeat clarithromycin, intensify acid suppression: double the PPI dose (e.g., omeprazole 40 mg BID) or use vonoprazan, which is not CYP2C19-dependent
C. Add clarithromycin 500 mg TID to increase H. pylori eradication
D. Use ranitidine instead of PPI as it has no CYP2C19 interaction
exp: CYP2C19 ultrarapid metabolizers (*17/*17) clear omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, and dexlansoprazole faster, which lowers PPI exposure and intragastric pH control and reduces H. pylori eradication. Higher intragastric pH improves amoxicillin and clarithromycin stability and activity and lets H. pylori enter the replicative, antibiotic-susceptible phase. CPIC 2020 recommends increasing the starting daily PPI dose by 100% for ultrarapid metabolizers being treated for H. pylori. Vonoprazan, a potassium-competitive acid blocker metabolized mainly by CYP3A4, gives potent acid suppression regardless of CYP2C19 genotype. ACG 2024 recommends avoiding repeat clarithromycin after a clarithromycin-based failure unless susceptibility is confirmed; bismuth quadruple therapy is the usual salvage regimen. A ignores the genotype finding; clarithromycin resistance may coexist, but standard-dose PPI will underperform in ultrarapid metabolizers. C is wrong because higher-dose clarithromycin does not overcome resistance or fix inadequate acid suppression. D is wrong because H2-receptor antagonists are inferior to PPIs in eradication regimens, and ranitidine was withdrawn from the US market in 2020.
ref: Vol 2 Drug Information; ACG H. pylori Guidelines 2017; CPIC CYP2C19 Guidelines
opts_exp: This ignores the actionable genotype. Clarithromycin resistance may coexist, but standard-dose omeprazole gives poor acid control in a CYP2C19 *17/*17 ultrarapid metabolizer and lowers eradication rates.

CPIC 2020 recommends increasing the starting daily PPI dose by 100% in ultrarapid metabolizers being treated for H. pylori, and vonoprazan, metabolized mainly by CYP3A4, suppresses acid potently regardless of CYP2C19 genotype. ACG 2024 advises avoiding repeat clarithromycin after a clarithromycin-based failure, with bismuth quadruple therapy as the usual salvage regimen.
Higher-dose clarithromycin does not overcome resistance or fix inadequate acid suppression, and ACG 2024 advises against repeating clarithromycin after failure unless susceptibility is confirmed.
H2-receptor antagonists are inferior to PPIs in H. pylori eradication regimens, and ranitidine was withdrawn from the US market in 2020.

q: A researcher reports that a new antibiotic reduced ICU-acquired infection rates compared to standard care: RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.56–0.91) in the per-protocol (PP) population, but RR 0.88 (95% CI 0.73–1.07) in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
opts: A. PP analysis is superior — it shows patients who actually took the drug, giving a purer efficacy signal
B. The ITT analysis is the primary analysis for efficacy — the non-significant ITT result suggests the drug may not be truly effective in clinical practice; PP provides explanatory insight only
C. The discordance proves protocol non-adherence was a confounder invalidating the study
D. Both analyses must be statistically significant for regulatory approval; since ITT is not, the drug cannot be approved
exp: INTENTION-TO-TREAT (ITT) vs PER-PROTOCOL (PP) analysis: ITT includes all randomized patients regardless of protocol adherence, preserving randomization and minimizing selection bias — it reflects 'real-world' effectiveness. PP includes only patients who completed treatment per protocol — it overestimates efficacy by excluding non-adherent patients (who may have not responded). REGULATORY: ITT is the gold standard for demonstrating efficacy in superiority trials. Non-significant ITT despite significant PP suggests the drug may not work when prescribed in real-world conditions (accounting for non-adherence, dropout, etc.). This discordance should NOT be dismissed — it is clinically meaningful. The PP can support biological plausibility, but the ITT conclusion drives practice.
ref: Vol 2 Drug Information/Biostatistics; FDA Guidance on ITT
opts_exp: A. PP analysis gives 'per-protocol efficacy' but introduces selection bias — patients who completed the protocol may differ systematically from those who did not (healthier, more adherent, fewer side effects). PP is explanatory (why did it work?), not confirmatory (does it work in practice?).

B. CORRECT. ITT preserves randomization integrity and reflects clinical practice (patients often don't take medications perfectly). Non-significant ITT (RR 0.88, CI includes 1.0) means no statistically significant benefit in the full clinical population. PP showing significance reflects best-case efficacy in adherent patients but not generalizable practice. The drug may have marginal real-world benefit.

C. Protocol non-adherence is expected and ITT is specifically designed to account for it. Discordance is informative, not invalidating. The study design is sound; interpretation requires acknowledging both analyses.

D. Not accurate — regulatory submission typically requires the pre-specified primary analysis (usually ITT for superiority) to be significant. However, regulatory decisions are nuanced; some approvals proceed with strong PP data if safety profile justifies. The statement as written (both must be significant) is not a regulatory standard.

q: A pharmacy director discovers that a nurse has been diverting hydromorphone from the Pyxis by removing vials labeled '4 mg/mL' and replacing them with similar-appearing morphine vials, then scanning the hydromorphone barcode during removal. This was discovered during a discrepancy audit showing 23 vials 'administered' but not documented in MAR over 6 weeks. Under DEA regulations, what is the reporting obligation and timeline?
opts: A. Report to State Board of Pharmacy within 30 days using DEA Form 41
B. Notify the local DEA field office in writing within one business day, and submit an accurate electronic DEA Form 106 within 45 days of discovery
C. Report internally to hospital administration and HR only — DEA notification is not required unless confirmed diversion by criminal charges
D. File DEA Form 222 within 15 days to document controlled substance loss
exp: The federal requirements distinguish initial written notification from the completed report: notify the local DEA field office within one business day of discovery of theft or significant loss, and submit an accurate electronic Form 106 within 45 days. Assess and fulfill separate state, licensing, law-enforcement, and institutional requirements without claiming a universal simultaneous state deadline.
ref: Vol 2 Healthcare Systems; 21 CFR 1301.76; DEA Diversion Control Division
opts_exp: A. DEA Form 41 is used for DESTRUCTION of controlled substances with a DEA-registered reverse distributor. Not applicable to theft/diversion. 30-day timeline for this form is incorrect.
B. Correct. Initial written DEA notification is due within one business day; the complete electronic Form 106 is due within 45 days. Separately determine applicable state and institutional duties.
C. Criminal charges are not required before reporting discovered theft or significant loss. Internal notification alone is insufficient.
D. DEA Form 222 is an ordering form for Schedule I/II substances from DEA-registered distributors. It has no role in reporting theft or diversion.
reviewNote: Targeted correction 2026-10-19; full chapter review pending.

q: A clinical pharmacist is evaluating a formulary request for sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) for HFrEF. In PARADIGM-HF, the primary outcome (CV death or HF hospitalization) occurred in 21.8% vs 26.5% of patients over a median 27 months (ARR 4.7%; NNT = 1/0.047 = 21.3, rounded up to 22). The drug costs $7,200/year vs enalapril at $180/year (annual cost difference $7,020). Which calculation correctly estimates the incremental drug cost per primary-outcome event prevented over the trial period?
opts: A. $7,020 (annual cost difference) ÷ 0.047 (ARR) = ~$149,000 per event prevented
B. ICER cannot be calculated without a QALY estimate; NNT-based ICER overestimates value
C. $7,200 ÷ 22 (NNT) = ~$327 per event prevented
D. $7,020/year × 2.25 years × 22 (NNT) = ~$347,000 per event prevented
exp: Cost per event prevented = incremental cost per patient over the period in which the ARR was observed × NNT. The ARR of 4.7% accrued over a median 27 months (2.25 years), so the incremental cost per patient over that period is $7,020 × 2.25 = $15,795. NNT = 1/0.047 = 21.3, rounded up to 22 (the PARADIGM-HF publication reported 21). Cost per event prevented = $15,795 × 22 = $347,490 (about $347,000). A treats the 27-month ARR as if it accrued in 1 year: $7,020 ÷ 0.047 = $149,362 counts only 1 year of drug cost, which underestimates the cost per event. B is wrong: an ICER can be expressed in natural units (cost per event prevented); QALYs are needed only for a cost-utility analysis. C divides cost by NNT instead of multiplying and uses the total rather than incremental cost. This figure counts drug acquisition cost only and ignores offsets from avoided hospitalizations. Published cost-utility analyses estimate about $45,000-$50,000 per QALY for sacubitril/valsartan (Gaziano et al. JAMA Cardiol 2016; Sandhu et al. Circulation 2016).
ref: Vol 2 Healthcare Systems; ISPOR Guidelines; PARADIGM-HF economic analyses
opts_exp: $7,020 ÷ 0.047 = about $149,000 counts only 1 year of drug cost, even though the 4.7% ARR accrued over a median 2.25 years, so it underestimates the cost per event prevented.
An ICER can be expressed in natural units such as cost per event prevented; a QALY estimate is needed only for a cost-utility analysis.
$7,200 ÷ 22 = about $327 divides by the NNT instead of multiplying and uses the total drug cost rather than the incremental cost over enalapril.

Incremental cost per patient over the trial period is $7,020 × 2.25 years = $15,795, and multiplying by the NNT of 22 gives $347,490, or about $347,000 per event prevented. This figure counts drug acquisition cost only and ignores offsets from avoided hospitalizations.

q: A health system pharmacy director is evaluating a biosimilar substitution policy for adalimumab biosimilars. Under FDA regulations and state pharmacy law, which statement correctly characterizes automatic substitution requirements?
opts: A. Any FDA-approved biosimilar can be automatically substituted for the reference biologic without prescriber notification

B. Only FDA-designated 'interchangeable' biosimilars may be automatically substituted; pharmacist must notify prescriber within a state-specified timeframe (commonly 5 business days) and document in patient record
C. Biosimilar substitution requires a new written prescription from the prescriber for each dispensing — cannot be auto-substituted regardless of FDA designation
D. Biosimilar substitution rules follow the same framework as generic drug substitution — any bioequivalent product can be substituted automatically without restriction
exp: Under the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act (BPCIA, 2010), the FDA licenses biosimilars (highly similar to the reference product, with no clinically meaningful differences) and may additionally designate a product as interchangeable. Only an interchangeable biosimilar may be substituted at the pharmacy without prescriber intervention, and only as permitted by state law. Most state substitution laws require the pharmacist to notify the prescriber within a set time (often within 5 business days, but this varies by state) and to document the dispensed product. A is wrong: biosimilars without interchangeable designation need prescriber authorization. C is wrong: interchangeable products can be substituted without a new prescription where state law allows. D is wrong: biologics are not 'generic equivalents' and follow a separate substitution framework. Interchangeability historically required switching studies; FDA's June 2024 draft guidance states that switching studies are generally no longer needed. Several adalimumab biosimilars (for example, Cyltezo, Abrilada, Simlandi) had interchangeable designation by 2024.
ref: Vol 2 Healthcare Systems; FDA BPCIA; NABP Model State Pharmacy Act
opts_exp: A biosimilar without interchangeable designation cannot be substituted at the pharmacy without prescriber authorization.

Under the BPCIA, only a biosimilar that FDA has designated interchangeable may be substituted without prescriber intervention, and only where state law allows. Most states require the pharmacist to notify the prescriber within a set time (often 5 business days, varying by state) and to document the product dispensed.
This is too restrictive; an interchangeable biosimilar can be substituted without a new prescription where state law permits.

Biologics are not generic equivalents and do not follow the small-molecule bioequivalence and generic substitution framework; substitution is limited to interchangeable products under state biosimilar laws.

q: A 58-year-old man with DM2, hypertension, CKD stage 3b (CrCl 32 mL/min), and a prior fluoroquinolone-associated Achilles tendon rupture presents with community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospitalization. He is not in the ICU, has no prior respiratory isolation of MRSA or P. aeruginosa, and has not been hospitalized or received IV antibiotics in the past 90 days. Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
opts: A. Azithromycin 500 mg PO daily
B. Levofloxacin 750 mg IV once, then 750 mg IV q48h (renally adjusted for CrCl 20-49 mL/min)
C. Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h + vancomycin IV
D. Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily
exp: For non-severe inpatient CAP without MRSA or P. aeruginosa risk factors, ATS/IDSA 2019 strongly recommends either a beta-lactam (ampicillin-sulbactam, cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, or ceftaroline) plus a macrolide, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy. Ceftriaxone 1-2 g daily plus azithromycin 500 mg daily needs no renal adjustment (ceftriaxone has dual renal and biliary elimination; azithromycin is hepatically cleared) and fits this patient. B is a correctly renally adjusted levofloxacin regimen, but a fluoroquinolone should be avoided after a prior fluoroquinolone-associated tendon rupture (FDA boxed warning), so it is not the best choice. C is wrong: ATS/IDSA 2019 recommends against empiric anti-MRSA and antipseudomonal coverage unless locally validated risk factors are present. A is wrong: macrolide monotherapy is only for selected outpatients, not hospitalized patients.
opts_exp: Macrolide monotherapy is reserved for selected outpatients with CAP and is not appropriate for a hospitalized patient with diabetes and CKD.

The levofloxacin dose is correctly adjusted for CrCl 32 mL/min, but a fluoroquinolone should be avoided after a prior fluoroquinolone-associated tendon rupture (FDA boxed warning), and an equally guideline-supported non-fluoroquinolone regimen is available.

ATS/IDSA 2019 recommends against empiric anti-MRSA and antipseudomonal coverage without locally validated risk factors, and he has none (no prior isolation, no hospitalization or IV antibiotics in 90 days). Vancomycin would also add nephrotoxicity risk in CKD 3b.

For non-severe inpatient CAP without MRSA or P. aeruginosa risk factors, ATS/IDSA 2019 strongly recommends a beta-lactam plus a macrolide. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin needs no renal adjustment, covers typical and atypical pathogens, and avoids a fluoroquinolone in this patient.

q: A patient with schizophrenia on clozapine 450 mg/day develops sudden worsening psychosis with clozapine level of 180 ng/mL (therapeutic range 350–600 ng/mL). Two weeks ago he started smoking 20 cigarettes/day after being smoke-free for 6 months. What is the mechanism and appropriate management?
opts: A. Clozapine is metabolized mainly by CYP1A2; polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A2 and increase clozapine clearance — increase the clozapine dose gradually (smokers often need about 1.5 times the nonsmoking dose) and monitor plasma levels weekly
B. Nicotine directly inhibits dopamine receptors, counteracting clozapine's antipsychotic mechanism — switch to olanzapine
C. Smoking reduces clozapine absorption by inducing P-glycoprotein efflux in GI tract
D. Smoking causes CYP3A4 induction, reducing clozapine levels — add fluvoxamine to inhibit CYP3A4
exp: Clozapine is metabolized mainly by CYP1A2, with minor contributions from CYP3A4, 2C19, and 2D6. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke, not nicotine, induce CYP1A2, so nicotine replacement does not cause this interaction. Starting to smoke can lower clozapine concentrations by roughly 30-50%, and smokers typically need about 1.5 times the dose of nonsmokers. Increase the dose stepwise, guided by symptoms and weekly plasma levels (target ≥350 ng/mL). If he stops smoking, induction wears off over about 1-2 weeks; the dose must then be reduced (often by about 30-40%) to avoid toxicity such as sedation, seizures, and orthostasis. B is wrong: nicotine does not block dopamine receptors in a way that negates clozapine, and switching agents is not needed for a PK problem. C is wrong: P-gp induction is not the mechanism. D is wrong on two counts: the relevant enzyme is CYP1A2, and fluvoxamine is a strong CYP1A2 inhibitor, not a CYP3A4-targeted strategy. Fluvoxamine augmentation is a specialist strategy, not first-line here.
ref: Vol 1 Psychiatry; Clozapine REMS Program; Drug Interactions Reference
opts_exp: Clozapine is cleared mainly by CYP1A2, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke (not nicotine) induce CYP1A2, lowering clozapine levels by roughly 30-50%. Increase the dose stepwise (smokers often need about 1.5 times the nonsmoking dose) with weekly levels toward at least 350 ng/mL, and reduce the dose if he stops smoking.

Nicotine does not block dopamine receptors in a way that negates clozapine; this is a pharmacokinetic problem, and switching to olanzapine would give up clozapine's efficacy in treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
P-glycoprotein induction in the gut is not the mechanism; the interaction is hepatic CYP1A2 induction by tobacco smoke.

The enzyme induced by smoking is CYP1A2, not CYP3A4, and fluvoxamine is a strong CYP1A2 inhibitor rather than a CYP3A4-targeted strategy; fluvoxamine augmentation is a specialist option, not first-line here.

q: A 45-year-old woman with lupus nephritis on mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 1500 mg BID, hydroxychloroquine, and prednisone reports new onset diarrhea and subtherapeutic MMF levels despite compliance. She was recently started on cholestyramine for dyslipidemia. What is the mechanism of this interaction?
opts: A. Cholestyramine chelates MMF in the GI tract, reducing absorption
B. Cholestyramine binds mycophenolic acid (MPA) and its glucuronide metabolite (MPAG) in enterohepatic circulation, interrupting recirculation and reducing systemic MPA exposure by 40%
C. Cholestyramine induces CYP3A4, increasing first-pass metabolism of MMF
D. Cholestyramine causes GI dysmotility accelerating MMF transit before absorption
exp: Mycophenolate mofetil undergoes: (1) Rapid hydrolysis to mycophenolic acid (MPA — the active immunosuppressant); (2) Glucuronidation to MPAG (inactive); (3) Enterohepatic RECYCLING — intestinal flora deconjugate MPAG back to MPA, which is reabsorbed. This enterohepatic cycling accounts for a secondary MPA peak at 6–12 hours and contributes 30–40% of total MPA AUC. Cholestyramine (bile acid sequestrant) binds MPAG in the intestinal lumen, PREVENTING its reabsorption → interrupts enterohepatic recirculation → reduces total MPA AUC by ~40%. This is a well-documented interaction reducing immunosuppression efficacy. Management: Avoid co-administration; separate by maximum time interval or substitute a different dyslipidemia agent (statin preferred in immunosuppressed patients).
opts_exp: A. Cholestyramine does not directly chelate the prodrug MMF — the interaction occurs at the level of mycophenolic acid glucuronide (MPAG) in the intestinal lumen during enterohepatic recirculation, not at absorption of the parent drug.

B. CORRECT. Cholestyramine binds MPAG (the glucuronide metabolite) in the gut, preventing deconjugation and reabsorption of MPA in enterohepatic cycling. This eliminates the secondary MPA peak and reduces total AUC by ~40%. This is clinically significant for transplant immunosuppression and lupus nephritis management.
C. MMF and MPA are not significantly metabolized by CYP3A4. MMF is converted by esterases; MPA is glucuronidated by UGT enzymes. Cholestyramine does not induce CYP enzymes.
D. While cholestyramine can cause GI side effects (diarrhea), the primary mechanistic explanation for reduced MPA levels is enterohepatic recirculation interruption, not transit time acceleration.

q: A patient with metastatic breast cancer on tamoxifen 20 mg/day also requires paroxetine for depression. Her oncologist notes concern. Which pharmacogenomic interaction should guide therapy?
opts: A. Paroxetine is a CYP2D6 substrate and inducer, increasing tamoxifen levels to toxic range
B. Paroxetine is a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor, reducing conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite endoxifen and potentially reducing efficacy; use venlafaxine (or escitalopram/citalopram) instead
C. Tamoxifen and paroxetine compete for CYP3A4 binding, causing additive QTc prolongation
D. Paroxetine increases estrogen receptor sensitivity, counteracting tamoxifen's antiestrogen mechanism
exp: Tamoxifen is a prodrug. Its main activation pathway is CYP3A4/5 N-demethylation to N-desmethyltamoxifen, which CYP2D6 then hydroxylates to endoxifen; CYP2D6 also forms 4-hydroxytamoxifen. Endoxifen and 4-hydroxytamoxifen are roughly 30-100 times more potent at the estrogen receptor than tamoxifen, and endoxifen is the main active metabolite because it circulates at higher concentrations. Paroxetine (like fluoxetine and bupropion) is a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor. It turns a normal metabolizer into a functional poor metabolizer and lowers endoxifen concentrations by about 64% (Stearns 2003). CPIC 2018 and NCCN advise avoiding strong and moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors with tamoxifen. Venlafaxine has minimal CYP2D6 inhibition and is the preferred antidepressant; escitalopram and citalopram (weak inhibitors) are reasonable alternatives. Sertraline and duloxetine are moderate inhibitors and are best avoided. A is wrong: paroxetine is a CYP2D6 inhibitor, not an inducer, and the interaction lowers active metabolite rather than causing toxicity. C is wrong: the key interaction is not CYP3A4 competition or QTc. D is wrong: paroxetine does not alter estrogen-receptor sensitivity.
ref: Vol 1 Oncology; CPIC CYP2D6 Tamoxifen Guideline 2018
opts_exp: Paroxetine inhibits CYP2D6; it is not an inducer. The interaction lowers active metabolite concentrations rather than causing tamoxifen toxicity.

Paroxetine is a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor that turns a normal metabolizer into a functional poor metabolizer and lowered endoxifen concentrations by about 64% (Stearns 2003), which may reduce tamoxifen efficacy. CPIC 2018 and NCCN advise avoiding strong and moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, so venlafaxine (minimal CYP2D6 inhibition) is preferred, with escitalopram or citalopram as alternatives.
The clinically important interaction is CYP2D6 inhibition reducing endoxifen formation, not CYP3A4 competition or additive QTc prolongation.
Paroxetine does not change estrogen receptor sensitivity; its interaction with tamoxifen is pharmacokinetic.

q: A 62-year-old patient with end-stage liver disease (MELD 24, Child-Pugh C) develops hepatic encephalopathy (HE) and is started on lactulose. He also requires treatment for a new diagnosis of C. difficile colitis (CDI). Which antibiotic therapy is most appropriate for his CDI given his hepatic dysfunction?
opts: A. Oral metronidazole 500 mg TID × 10 days (first-line for mild CDI)
B. Oral vancomycin 125 mg QID × 10 days
C. Oral rifaximin 550 mg BID × 10 days (already appropriate for his HE and poorly absorbed)
D. IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h
exp: The IDSA/SHEA 2021 CDI focused update recommends fidaxomicin (preferred) or oral vancomycin 125 mg QID × 10 days for an initial episode. Metronidazole is no longer recommended as first-line therapy; it is reserved for nonsevere CDI when neither agent is available. Oral vancomycin is the only guideline-recommended agent among these options. It is minimally absorbed from the gut and needs no hepatic adjustment, so it is a good choice in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis. Fidaxomicin would be equally acceptable but is not offered. A is wrong: metronidazole is no longer first-line for mild CDI. It is also hepatically cleared, the label advises a 50% dose reduction in severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment, and accumulation can cause neurotoxicity that could be confused with or worsen HE. C is wrong: rifaximin is indicated for HE but is not recommended for treating an initial CDI episode. Its only CDI role is as an adjunct (vancomycin followed by rifaximin) for recurrent disease. D is wrong: IV metronidazole is used only as an adjunct to oral/rectal vancomycin in fulminant CDI and has the same hepatic concerns.
topic: Infectious Disease - CDI Treatment in Liver Disease
opts_exp: Metronidazole is no longer first-line for CDI of any severity per IDSA/SHEA 2021. It is also hepatically cleared, the label advises a 50% dose reduction in Child-Pugh C, and accumulation can cause neurotoxicity that may mimic or worsen hepatic encephalopathy.

IDSA/SHEA 2021 recommends fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin 125 mg QID for 10 days for an initial CDI episode, and oral vancomycin is the only guideline-recommended agent offered. It is minimally absorbed and needs no hepatic adjustment, which suits Child-Pugh C cirrhosis.
Rifaximin is indicated for hepatic encephalopathy but is not recommended for an initial CDI episode; its only CDI role is as an adjunct after vancomycin for recurrent disease.
IV metronidazole is used only as an adjunct to oral or rectal vancomycin in fulminant CDI, and it carries the same hepatic and neurotoxicity concerns in this patient.

q: A patient with systolic heart failure (EF 30%) on sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg BID, carvedilol 25 mg BID, and spironolactone 25 mg daily is hospitalized for acute decompensation. On day 3, he is euvolemic but remains hypotensive (BP 75/45 mmHg, MAP 55 mmHg) with lightheadedness on sitting up and HR 56 bpm. Extremities are warm, lactate is normal, and urine output is adequate. Serum potassium is 5.9 mEq/L. Which medication adjustment is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A. Stop carvedilol, reduce sacubitril/valsartan to 24/26 mg BID
B. Stop spironolactone only; continue sacubitril/valsartan and carvedilol at current doses
C. Hold all three neurohormonal agents temporarily; when hemodynamically stable (MAP >65), restart at lower doses with careful up-titration
D. Add midodrine 10 mg TID for persistent hypotension
exp: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline supports continuing GDMT during HF hospitalization unless there is hemodynamic instability or a contraindication. This patient has both. He has symptomatic hypotension (MAP 55) with relative bradycardia (HR 56), and his potassium of 5.9 mEq/L requires stopping the MRA (MRAs are held when K >5.5). Each agent contributes to the low BP: the ARNI by vasodilation, carvedilol through beta-blockade, alpha-1 blockade, and slower heart rate, and spironolactone through hyperkalemia. Temporarily holding all three is appropriate. Once MAP is >65 and K has normalized, restart at low doses and re-titrate, starting with the beta-blocker and ARNI and adding the MRA back when K is <5.0. Perfusion is preserved (warm, normal lactate, adequate urine output), so inotropes or vasopressors are not needed. A is wrong: it leaves spironolactone running at K 5.9. B is wrong: keeping full-dose ARNI and carvedilol with MAP 55 and HR 56 will sustain the symptomatic hypotension. D is wrong: midodrine treats the symptom with a vasopressor while leaving the causative drugs and the hyperkalemia unaddressed, and it has no role in HFrEF GDMT.
topic: Cardiology - Acute Decompensated HF Medication Management
ref: Vol 1 Acute Care Cardiology; ACC/AHA HF Guidelines 2022
opts_exp: This leaves spironolactone running with a potassium of 5.9 mEq/L and keeps a vasodilating ARNI going at a MAP of 55, so it does not fully address either problem.
Stopping spironolactone treats the hyperkalemia, but continuing full-dose sacubitril/valsartan and carvedilol with a MAP of 55 and HR of 56 will sustain the symptomatic hypotension and bradycardia.

He has symptomatic hypotension (MAP 55) with relative bradycardia, and a potassium of 5.9 mEq/L exceeds the 5.5 threshold for holding an MRA, so temporarily holding all three agents is appropriate; perfusion is preserved, so inotropes are not needed. Once MAP is above 65, restart the beta-blocker and ARNI at low doses and add the MRA back when potassium is below 5.0.
Midodrine treats the low blood pressure with a vasopressor while leaving the causative drugs and the hyperkalemia unaddressed, and it has no role in HFrEF GDMT.

q: A patient taking rivaroxaban presents with disabling acute ischemic stroke, and imaging confirms a treatable large-vessel occlusion. Which principle is correct?
opts: A. Recent DOAC exposure automatically excludes mechanical thrombectomy
B. Do not delay thrombectomy assessment to reverse rivaroxaban solely for the procedure
C. Andexanet must always precede thrombectomy
D. Wait 24 hours regardless of imaging and deficits
exp: Mechanical thrombectomy eligibility should be assessed urgently; DOAC reversal is not routinely required solely to perform it. IV thrombolysis is a separate decision requiring current protocols and expert assessment.
ref: Vol 1 Neurology; AHA/ASA 2023 Ischemic Stroke Guidelines; Andexanet Alfa PI
opts_exp: A. Recent DOAC use does not automatically exclude mechanical thrombectomy.

B. Correct. Mechanical thrombectomy eligibility should be assessed urgently; DOAC reversal is not routinely required solely to perform it. IV thrombolysis is a separate decision requiring current protocols and expert assessment.
C. Routine andexanet before thrombectomy is not required, and reversal to enable IV thrombolysis is not routinely recommended.
D. A fixed delay forfeits time-sensitive reperfusion opportunities.
reviewNote: Targeted correction 2026-10-19; full chapter review pending.

q: A study reports a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.68 (95% CI 0.51–0.91) for time to first hospitalization with Drug C versus placebo over 36 months. Kaplan-Meier curves separate at 3 months and remain separated throughout. Which statement is most accurate about this finding?
opts: A. Drug C reduces the absolute rate of hospitalization by 32%

B. HR 0.68 indicates Drug C is associated with a 32% REDUCTION in the instantaneous HAZARD of hospitalization at any given time point, in the drug group vs. placebo — the event rate ratio at any moment
C. HR 0.68 means patients on Drug C have a 68% probability of avoiding hospitalization
D. The HR of 0.68 is equivalent to RR 0.68 since the outcome is time-to-event
exp: Hazard ratio interpretation: HR = ratio of hazard RATES (instantaneous event probability) in treatment vs. control at any given time point, assuming proportional hazards. HR 0.68 = Drug C associated with 32% LOWER hazard of hospitalization at any instant in time compared to placebo. Importantly: HR ≠ RR (relative risk). RR is a cumulative probability comparison over a fixed time period. HR is a time-dependent rate ratio. HR ≠ absolute risk reduction (ARR = difference in cumulative event rates at a specified time). HR ≠ probability of avoiding hospitalization. When Kaplan-Meier curves separate early and remain separated (proportional hazards assumption likely met), HR interpretation across the study period is reliable. BCPS tests ability to distinguish HR from RR and ARR.
opts_exp: A. HR 0.68 is a RELATIVE measure (rate ratio). Absolute risk reduction requires knowing baseline event rates and cannot be derived from HR alone.

B. CORRECT. HR = instantaneous hazard rate ratio (Drug C : Placebo). HR 0.68 = 32% reduction in the hazard at any moment. Under proportional hazards assumption, this ratio is constant across the follow-up period. HR is neither a probability nor an absolute difference.
C. HR 0.68 does not represent probability of avoiding an event. That would be derived from survival function S(t) at a specific time point.

D. HR and RR are different statistics even when >0.8 (when rare events exist, they approximate). HR is event rate ratio (time-to-event analysis); RR is cumulative incidence ratio at a fixed time. They differ when event rates are not constant over time.

q: A clinical pharmacist reviews a crossover study of Drug D in 24 patients with migraine. Each patient received Drug D and placebo in random order with a 2-week washout period. The primary outcome is pain score (0–10) at 2 hours. Paired t-test: p=0.03. Mean difference = 1.8 points. What is the critical limitation that could invalidate this design?
opts: A. Crossover design is not valid for migraine studies — only parallel-group RCTs are appropriate
B. Insufficient washout period if Drug D has a long half-life or prolonged pharmacodynamic effects, leading to carryover effects contaminating the second period
C. Paired t-test is inappropriate for crossover data — only ANOVA can be used
D. N=24 is too small to detect a clinically meaningful difference in migraine pain
exp: Crossover design advantages: each patient serves as their own control (eliminates inter-patient variability), requires fewer patients, paired analysis. Critical limitation: CARRYOVER EFFECT — if Drug D has prolonged effects (long half-life, sustained pharmacodynamic effect) that persist into the second period, they contaminate the second observation, biasing results. Mitigation: adequate washout period (5 half-lives for PK washout; longer for PD effects). If migraine episodes resolve spontaneously (period effect) or Drug D prevents future attacks (sustained benefit), washout is inadequate. Crossover designs ARE valid for stable, recurrent conditions (migraine qualifies as a recurring, relatively stable disease). Paired t-test IS appropriate for crossover data (each patient has a pair of observations). N=24 may be adequate with crossover design's efficiency gains.
opts_exp: A. Crossover designs ARE used in migraine research — they are particularly suited to stable, episodic conditions where the same patient can experience multiple attacks over time. Parallel groups are not the only valid design.

B. CORRECT. Carryover effect is the critical threat to crossover validity. If Drug D's effects persist after the washout period into the second study period, the assumption of independent periods is violated. The 2-week washout must exceed both pharmacokinetic (5 half-lives) and pharmacodynamic washout. If carryover occurs, the crossover may need to be analyzed as a parallel design using only first-period data.

C. Paired t-test is appropriate for crossover data when comparing two periods (treatment vs. placebo in the same patient = paired observations). ANOVA is used for crossover designs with >2 periods but is not required for a two-period study.

D. N=24 is small for a parallel RCT but crossover designs gain power by eliminating between-patient variance. N=24 may be adequately powered for a clinically meaningful 1.8-point difference in pain score.

q: A pharmacist is reviewing a drug interaction between warfarin and a new herbal supplement containing St. John's Wort. The patient's INR dropped from 2.8 to 1.4. Which mechanism best explains the interaction?
opts: A. St. John's Wort directly binds warfarin in the intestinal lumen, preventing absorption
B. Hyperforin (active constituent) activates Pregnane X receptor (PXR), inducing CYP2C9, CYP3A4, and P-glycoprotein — dramatically increasing warfarin metabolism and decreasing plasma levels
C. St. John's Wort causes additive anticoagulant effects, reducing warfarin requirements
D. Hypericin in St. John's Wort inhibits CYP2C9, reducing S-warfarin clearance
exp: St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) contains hyperforin (primary CYP/P-gp inducer) and hypericin (antidepressant activity). MECHANISM: Hyperforin activates Pregnane X receptor (PXR) — a nuclear receptor transcription factor that upregulates CYP2C9, CYP3A4, P-glycoprotein, and other metabolic enzymes. S-warfarin (the more potent enantiomer) is metabolized primarily by CYP2C9; R-warfarin by CYP3A4. Induction of both enzymes dramatically increases warfarin clearance → reduced plasma levels → subtherapeutic INR. This is one of the most clinically significant herb-drug interactions. Onset: 2–3 weeks. P-gp induction also reduces oral drug absorption of P-gp substrates. Management: avoid co-administration with narrow therapeutic index drugs. If St. John's Wort started: monitor INR closely and increase warfarin dose. If stopped: anticipate INR increase and reduce warfarin dose.
ref: Vol 2 Drug Information; Natural Medicines Database
opts_exp: A. St. John's Wort does not bind warfarin directly. The interaction is pharmacokinetic (enzyme induction), not a physical binding/chelation interaction.

B. CORRECT. Hyperforin activates PXR, the master regulator of drug metabolism. PXR activation induces CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 (both warfarin metabolizers) plus P-gp. Result: warfarin clearance increases 2–3 fold, INR decreases significantly (as seen: 2.8 → 1.4). This is an INDUCTION interaction — the opposite of inhibition.
C. St. John's Wort has NO anticoagulant effect. It REDUCES warfarin levels through enzyme induction. The INR drop confirms reduced anticoagulation.
D. Hypericin is the antidepressant/photosensitizing constituent but is NOT the primary CYP interactor. Hyperforin is responsible for CYP induction. Hypericin does not significantly inhibit CYP2C9.

q: A hospital P&T committee is evaluating a new monoclonal antibody costing $45,000/infusion. The manufacturer's pharmacoeconomic model shows ICER of $85,000/QALY using a 3% discount rate and 10-year time horizon. An independent analysis using 5% discount rate and 5-year horizon calculates ICER of $142,000/QALY. Which explanation best accounts for the discordant ICERs?
opts: A. Higher discount rate reduces the present value of future benefits more than costs, increasing ICER; shorter time horizon may not capture full long-term benefit accrual, further increasing ICER
B. The manufacturer's model is fraudulent — independent analyses always produce higher ICERs
C. A 5-year horizon is always more accurate because long-term models are speculative
D. The 5% discount rate only affects costs, not benefits — hence the ICER increase is purely cost-driven
exp: Pharmacoeconomic modeling: ICER discordance from discount rate and time horizon differences: (1) DISCOUNT RATE: Future benefits and costs are discounted to present value. Higher discount rate (5% vs 3%) penalizes future benefits more steeply. For chronic conditions where clinical benefits (QALYs) accrue over years while costs occur early, a higher discount rate proportionally reduces the PRESENT VALUE of delayed benefits more than upfront drug costs → ICER increases. (2) TIME HORIZON: Shorter horizon (5 vs 10 years) may not capture: downstream cost offsets (fewer hospitalizations, reduced complications); full QALY accrual from disease modification. If the drug prevents expensive late complications (year 5–10), a 5-year horizon misses these savings → ICER rises. Both factors operating together explain the discordance ($85K→$142K).
ref: Vol 2 Healthcare Systems; ISPOR Good Practices for Outcomes Research
opts_exp: A. CORRECT. Higher discount rate: future QALYs are discounted more heavily than near-term drug costs → denominator (QALY gain) shrinks in present value terms more than numerator (incremental cost) → ICER increases. Shorter time horizon misses long-term cost offsets and QALY benefits → further increases ICER. Both factors operating simultaneously explain the jump from $85K to $142K/QALY.

B. Industry bias in pharmacoeconomic models is a legitimate concern, but independent analyses do not 'always' produce higher ICERs. The discordance here is methodologically explainable by discount rate and time horizon differences — these are sensitivity analysis parameters, not fraud indicators.

C. Model time horizon selection depends on the disease trajectory and drug mechanism. For chronic disease-modifying therapies, longer horizons capturing full benefit accrual are more appropriate (and more conservative from a cost-effectiveness standpoint). 5-year horizon is not always superior.

D. Discount rates apply to BOTH costs and benefits (QALYs). The differential effect arises because costs and benefits occur at different times in the model — higher rates disproportionately reduce the present value of delayed benefits versus upfront costs.

q: A pharmacy director performs root cause analysis after a patient received 10× the intended insulin dose from a computerized order system. The error chain included: ambiguous order (5 units written as '5U' misread as '50'), no independent double-check, and a CPOE alert overridden 3 times. Under a Just Culture framework, how should the nurse who overrode the alert three times be managed?
opts: A. Immediate termination — three overrides of a safety alert is reckless behavior requiring punitive action

B. Evaluate intent and context: if the overrides represent 'alert fatigue' from low-specificity alerts (nuisance alerts), the system design is the root cause — coaching + alert optimization, not punishment
C. Mandatory retraining on insulin safety only — individual education is the primary intervention
D. The nurse is fully responsible as a licensed professional — system factors do not mitigate individual accountability
exp: JUST CULTURE framework (David Marx): Distinguishes between human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior: (1) Human error (inadvertent): console/support — system redesign; (2) At-risk behavior (behavioral choice not recognizing risk, e.g., normalized alert override due to alert fatigue): COACHING, not punishment — and system redesign to reduce alert fatigue (specificity improvement); (3) Reckless behavior (conscious disregard of substantial risk): punitive action. Alert fatigue is a SYSTEMS-LEVEL problem — when CPOE generates excessive nuisance alerts (low specificity), clinicians normalize overriding them (at-risk behavior, not reckless). Root cause = system design (alert architecture). The nurse likely engaged in at-risk behavior (alert fatigue), not reckless behavior. Just Culture: individual coaching on alert significance + SYSTEM FIX (reduce low-value alerts, add hard-stop for insulin dose multiples). Institutional accountability lies with the system design, not solely the individual.
ref: Vol 2 Healthcare Systems; Just Culture (David Marx); IHI Patient Safety Resources
opts_exp: A. Immediate termination reflects a 'blame culture' approach — punishing individuals without addressing systemic root causes. This does not prevent future errors and may discourage error reporting.

B. CORRECT. Just Culture differentiates at-risk behavior (alert override due to normalized fatigue) from reckless behavior. Alert fatigue from low-specificity CPOE alerts is a known systems problem. The appropriate response: counsel the nurse, AND fix the alert system (increase specificity, add hard-stop for high-risk medications like insulin). System redesign prevents recurrence more effectively than punishment.

C. Individual retraining alone is insufficient per high-reliability organization (HRO) and Just Culture principles. Without addressing the system (alert fatigue), the same at-risk behavior will recur. Retraining is a component but not the primary intervention.

D. While individual accountability exists, Just Culture explicitly recognizes that systems design influences behavior. Attributing full responsibility to the individual without system analysis misses the prevention opportunity and violates Just Culture principles.

q: A hospital implements a pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship program (ASP). Six months after implementation, broad-spectrum antibiotic use decreased by 30% (DDD/1000 patient-days) but C. difficile infection rates increased 12%. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: A. ASP interventions disrupted the microbiome, directly causing C. difficile overgrowth in all patients
B. C. difficile rate increase suggests the ASP increased broad-spectrum use in a subset of patients, causing paradoxical harm

C. A factor outside the ASP is more likely, such as a change in CDI testing (e.g., switch to stand-alone PCR/NAAT), transmission of a hypervirulent strain (BI/NAP1/027), or lapses in infection prevention; reduced antibiotic exposure should not by itself raise CDI rates
D. ASP programs always cause short-term C. difficile increases before long-term improvement — this is expected and requires no action
exp: Antibiotic exposure is the main modifiable risk factor for CDI, and the IDSA/SHEA 2016 ASP guideline lists CDI reduction as an expected stewardship benefit. A 30% fall in broad-spectrum use alongside a rise in CDI therefore points to a cause outside the ASP. Common causes are a change in laboratory testing (moving to a more sensitive stand-alone NAAT/PCR raises reported CDI because it detects colonization), an outbreak of a hypervirulent strain such as ribotype 027 (fluoroquinolone-resistant, binary toxin-producing), lapses in hand hygiene, contact precautions, or sporicidal cleaning, and changes in case mix or denominators. The right response is to investigate: review testing practices, infection prevention audits, and strain typing. A is wrong: less antibiotic exposure does not disrupt the microbiome more, and 'all patients' is absolute. B is wrong: it contradicts the measured 30% drop in broad-spectrum use. D is wrong: stewardship programs do not reliably cause transient CDI increases, and an unexplained rise always needs investigation.
ref: Vol 2 Healthcare Systems; IDSA/SHEA ASP Guidelines 2016
opts_exp: Less antibiotic exposure does not disrupt the microbiome more, and the claim that it caused CDI in all patients is absolute and implausible.
This contradicts the measured 30% fall in broad-spectrum antibiotic use, so it cannot explain the CDI increase.

Antibiotic exposure is the main modifiable CDI risk factor, so a 30% drop in broad-spectrum use should lower CDI, not raise it. A concurrent outside factor is more likely, such as a switch to stand-alone NAAT/PCR that detects colonization, a ribotype 027 outbreak, or lapses in hand hygiene, contact precautions, or sporicidal cleaning, and it should be investigated.
Stewardship programs do not reliably cause transient CDI increases, and any unexplained rise needs investigation of testing, infection prevention, and strain typing.

q: During a formulary review, a P&T committee member argues that a drug should be approved because it received accelerated FDA approval. The clinical pharmacist member should clarify which of the following?
opts: A. Accelerated approval means full Phase III data confirmed efficacy — the drug has rigorous clinical evidence

B. Accelerated approval uses a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit; post-marketing confirmatory trials are required to verify actual clinical benefit — formulary decisions should weigh this uncertainty
C. Accelerated approval drugs have the same evidence standard as regular approval but achieve it faster
D. Accelerated approval is only granted for oncology drugs and cannot apply to other therapeutic areas
exp: FDA ACCELERATED APPROVAL PATHWAY (21 CFR 314.500 / 601.40): Grants approval based on SURROGATE or INTERMEDIATE CLINICAL ENDPOINT (biomarker, imaging finding, lab value) reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit — NOT actual clinical outcomes (survival, morbidity). Example: tumor response rate (surrogate) vs. overall survival (clinical benefit). REQUIREMENT: Post-marketing confirmatory trials to verify actual clinical benefit must be completed with due diligence. Sponsor can be required to complete within specified timeframe (accelerated approval reform 2022). FORMULARY IMPLICATIONS: Surrogate endpoints may not translate to clinical benefit — multiple accelerated approval drugs have been withdrawn when confirmatory trials showed no survival benefit (e.g., several oncology agents). P&T should: assess surrogate endpoint validity, timing of confirmatory trial, strength of biological plausibility, and risk/benefit in the specific patient population. Accelerated approval covers ALL therapeutic areas (not only oncology), including HIV, rare diseases.
ref: Vol 2 Drug Information/Healthcare Systems; FDA Accelerated Approval Program
opts_exp: A. Accelerated approval specifically does NOT require full Phase III confirmatory data before approval — that is the entire point of the pathway. It expedites access by accepting surrogate endpoints pending confirmatory evidence.

B. CORRECT. Accelerated approval = surrogate/intermediate endpoint approval with mandatory post-marketing confirmatory trials. The clinical benefit remains to be confirmed. P&T should not treat accelerated approval as equivalent evidence to full approval — the uncertainty about clinical benefit should factor into formulary decisions, coverage restrictions, and monitoring requirements.
C. Accelerated approval is faster but also has a LOWER evidence standard (surrogate vs. clinical endpoint) — not the same standard achieved faster.
D. Accelerated approval applies broadly: oncology, HIV/AIDS, rare diseases, and increasingly other areas. It is not limited to oncology.

q: A 19-year-old female college student presents with 4 days of progressive sore throat, fever (38.9°C), and fatigue. Exam reveals markedly enlarged tonsils with white exudates, posterior cervical and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy, and mild left upper quadrant discomfort on palpation. She has no known drug allergies. The on-call provider prescribes amoxicillin 500 mg TID. Two days later she develops a diffuse pruritic maculopapular rash over her trunk and extremities. She denies shortness of breath, tongue or lip swelling, wheezing, nausea, or vomiting. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A. Administer epinephrine 0.3 mg IM and start diphenhydramine — anaphylaxis to amoxicillin

B. Stop amoxicillin and obtain a monospot (heterophile antibody) test; the rash is the expected non-allergic amoxicillin reaction in EBV mononucleosis, so she should not be labeled penicillin-allergic (an oral antihistamine may be used only for symptomatic itch)
C. Switch to azithromycin for penicillin-class allergy to cover atypical organisms
D. Continue amoxicillin and add prednisone to suppress the allergic rash
exp: This is EBV mononucleosis misdiagnosed as strep pharyngitis. Posterior cervical and posterior auricular adenopathy, marked fatigue, and LUQ tenderness (splenomegaly) favor mono; strep typically causes anterior cervical adenopathy. Aminopenicillins given during EBV infection cause a maculopapular rash, historically reported in up to 80-100% of patients and in about 30% in more recent series. It is a transient, virus-associated reaction and not IgE-mediated allergy. She has no urticaria, angioedema, respiratory, or GI symptoms. Management: stop amoxicillin, confirm with a heterophile antibody test (EBV-specific antibodies if negative), and give supportive care. An oral antihistamine is acceptable for itch but is not treating an allergy. She should not carry a penicillin-allergy label, and she should avoid contact sports for at least 3-4 weeks because of splenic rupture risk. A is wrong: there are no signs of anaphylaxis. C is wrong: there is no true allergy, and an antibiotic does not treat viral mono. D is wrong: continuing amoxicillin prolongs the rash, and steroids are not indicated for the rash.
topic: Infectious Disease - Killer Foil: Mono vs. Strep
ref: Vol 1 Infectious Diseases; Part 3: Red Flags & Killer Foils (High-Yield Med Reviews)
opts_exp: There are no signs of anaphylaxis (no urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, hypotension, or GI symptoms), so epinephrine is not indicated.

Posterior cervical and posterior auricular adenopathy, marked fatigue, and LUQ tenderness point to EBV mononucleosis, and the aminopenicillin rash in EBV is a transient, non-IgE-mediated reaction. Stop amoxicillin, confirm with a heterophile antibody test, avoid a penicillin-allergy label, and advise no contact sports for at least 3-4 weeks because of splenic rupture risk.
There is no true penicillin allergy, and an antibiotic does not treat viral mononucleosis; switching would also reinforce an incorrect allergy label.
Continuing amoxicillin prolongs the rash and treats a viral illness with an antibiotic, and corticosteroids are not indicated for this rash.

q: A 74-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation is started on amiodarone 400 mg daily to maintain sinus rhythm. His current medications include warfarin 5 mg daily (INR 2.4 on last check 2 weeks ago), digoxin 0.125 mg daily (level 0.9 ng/mL), and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. What medication adjustments are most critical at this time?
opts: A. No changes needed — amiodarone interactions are only clinically relevant at higher doses
B. Reduce warfarin dose by approximately 30-50%, reduce digoxin dose by approximately 50%, and monitor INR and digoxin levels closely within 1-2 weeks
C. Stop warfarin immediately — amiodarone provides antithrombotic coverage; reduce digoxin by 25%
D. Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg (amiodarone reduces statin efficacy); no changes to warfarin or digoxin needed
exp: RED FLAG DRUG: Amiodarone. This is one of the most clinically important drug interactions on BPS exams. MECHANISMS: (1) Warfarin interaction: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9 (metabolizes S-warfarin, the more potent enantiomer) AND CYP3A4 (R-warfarin). Result: warfarin levels increase dramatically → INR rises. Expected INR increase: 30-50% or more. Reduce warfarin dose by 30-50% when starting amiodarone. Monitor INR frequently (weekly initially). Onset: 1-3 weeks (amiodarone has weeks-long half-life, so effect builds gradually). (2) Digoxin interaction: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein (P-gp), reducing digoxin renal tubular secretion, AND reduces digoxin Vd. Digoxin levels rise 70-100%. Reduce digoxin dose by 50% when amiodarone is added. Monitor digoxin levels. (3) Atorvastatin: Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp, potentially increasing statin levels. HOWEVER, increasing statin dose is contraindicated — not needed. Monitor for myopathy.
ref: Vol 1 Cardiology; Part 3: Red Flags & Killer Foils (High-Yield Med Reviews)
opts_exp: A. WRONG. Amiodarone drug interactions are clinically critical at ALL doses due to its CYP2C9, CYP3A4, and P-gp inhibition. The extremely long half-life means effects accumulate over weeks. Failure to reduce warfarin leads to supratherapeutic INR and bleeding risk.

B. CORRECT. Both warfarin (CYP2C9/3A4 inhibition → ↑ INR) and digoxin (P-gp inhibition → ↑ digoxin levels) require dose reductions. Warfarin: reduce by 30-50% and recheck INR in 1-2 weeks. Digoxin: reduce by ~50% and recheck level in 1-2 weeks. These are the two most critical interactions to manage immediately upon amiodarone initiation.

C. Warfarin should NOT be stopped — amiodarone has no antithrombotic effect. Stopping anticoagulation in AF increases stroke risk significantly. The warfarin interaction requires DOSE REDUCTION, not discontinuation. The digoxin dose reduction of 25% is insufficient — 50% is appropriate.

D. INCREASING atorvastatin is CONTRAINDICATED — amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4, which would INCREASE atorvastatin exposure, raising myopathy risk. Statin dose should be capped or reduced with amiodarone. Ignoring the warfarin/digoxin interactions is dangerous.

q: A 58-year-old man presents for routine follow-up. He has type 2 diabetes (A1c 7.8%), hypertension (BP 148/88), heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 32%), and CKD stage 3b (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m²). His medications include metformin 500 mg BID (reduced last year for his eGFR), lisinopril 10 mg daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg BID, and furosemide 40 mg daily. His potassium is 4.8 mEq/L and serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL. He has no current urinary symptoms. Which medication change would MOST comprehensively address his cardiovascular-renal-metabolic risk?
opts: A. Add spironolactone 25 mg daily for HFrEF (mortality benefit), recognizing K must be monitored closely given K 4.8 and CKD
B. Switch metformin to a GLP-1 receptor agonist for better glycemic control in CKD

C. Add an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin or dapagliflozin) — provides HFrEF mortality benefit (HHF reduction), CKD progression protection, and cardiovascular risk reduction; eGFR 38 is above threshold for HF/CKD indications
D. Increase lisinopril to 40 mg (maximum dose) for optimal RAS blockade in HFrEF
exp: This patient has T2DM, HTN, HFrEF, and CKD 3b. An SGLT2 inhibitor is the single change that addresses all of them. In HFrEF it reduced CV death or HF hospitalization (DAPA-HF, NNT about 21 over 18 months; EMPEROR-Reduced). It slows CKD progression (CREDENCE with canagliflozin, DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY), and it provides modest glucose lowering and CV risk reduction in T2DM. eGFR 38 is above the initiation thresholds for the HF/CKD indications (empagliflozin eGFR ≥20; dapagliflozin eGFR ≥25). The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline gives SGLT2i a Class 1 recommendation in HFrEF, and KDIGO 2022 and ADA 2024 recommend them for T2DM with CKD. A is reasonable HFrEF GDMT (an MRA is recommended when eGFR >30 and K <5.0), but it does nothing for glycemia or CKD progression, and K 4.8 with CKD 3b carries real hyperkalemia risk. It is less comprehensive. B is wrong: GLP-1 RAs have no proven benefit in HFrEF (FIGHT was neutral with a trend toward harm), and stopping metformin is not needed at eGFR 38 at a reduced dose. D is wrong: uptitrating the ACE inhibitor is reasonable but addresses only one pillar and does not add the cardiorenal benefit of an SGLT2i. (Metformin is limited to 1,000 mg/day at eGFR 30-44 per FDA labeling and ADA/KDIGO.)
ref: Vol 1 HF/Vol 2 Endocrine; EMPEROR-Reduced; DAPA-HF; ACC/AHA 2022 HF Guidelines
opts_exp: Spironolactone is reasonable HFrEF therapy (eGFR above 30 and K below 5.0), but it does nothing for glycemia or CKD progression, and a potassium of 4.8 with CKD 3b carries real hyperkalemia risk, so it is less comprehensive.

GLP-1 receptor agonists have no proven benefit in HFrEF (FIGHT was neutral with a trend toward harm), and metformin does not need to be stopped at eGFR 38 at its reduced dose (limit 1,000 mg/day at eGFR 30-44).

An SGLT2 inhibitor reduces CV death or HF hospitalization in HFrEF (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced), slows CKD progression (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY), and adds modest glucose lowering. eGFR 38 is above the initiation thresholds (empagliflozin 20 or higher, dapagliflozin 25 or higher), and AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022, KDIGO 2022, and ADA 2024 all recommend it.
Uptitrating lisinopril is reasonable but addresses only RAS blockade and does not add the heart failure, renal, and metabolic benefits of an SGLT2 inhibitor.

q: A randomized controlled trial of a new antihypertensive drug reports: Treatment group: 18% 5-year cardiovascular event rate. Placebo group: 24% 5-year cardiovascular event rate. Which of the following statements about this trial result is INCORRECT?
opts: A. The absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 6% (24% - 18%)
B. The relative risk reduction (RRR) is 25% (6/24)
C. The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one cardiovascular event over 5 years is approximately 17
D. The relative risk (RR) of 0.75 means there is a 75% absolute reduction in cardiovascular events with treatment
exp: NEGATIVE QUESTION TYPE: Identify the FALSE statement. Strategy: evaluate each as a T/F statement — the FALSE one is correct. Calculations: ARR = 24% - 18% = 6% (A: TRUE). RRR = ARR/Control rate = 6%/24% = 25% (B: TRUE). NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.06 = 16.7 ≈ 17 (C: TRUE). Statement D: RR = treatment rate/control rate = 18%/24% = 0.75. RR 0.75 means the treatment group has 75% of the EVENT RATE of the placebo group — i.e., a 25% RELATIVE reduction (not 75%). Saying 'RR 0.75 = 75% absolute reduction' is INCORRECT. The absolute reduction is 6%. D is the FALSE statement → correct answer. KEY TRAP: RR 0.75 does NOT equal '75% absolute reduction.' RR 0.75 = 25% RRR. RR 0.25 would mean a 75% relative risk reduction. Students commonly confuse RR value with percentage reduction.
ref: Vol 2 Drug Information/Biostatistics; BPS Test-Taking Strategies Part 1
opts_exp: A. ARR = 24% - 18% = 6%. This is TRUE — it is the absolute difference in event rates between groups over 5 years. Not the answer.
B. RRR = ARR/control rate = 6%/24% = 0.25 = 25%. This is TRUE. Not the answer.
C. NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.06 = 16.7 ≈ 17. This is TRUE. Not the answer.

D. INCORRECT (= correct answer for negative question). RR 0.75 means the treatment group has 75% of the risk of the control group — i.e., a 25% RELATIVE risk reduction. It does NOT mean a 75% absolute reduction. The absolute reduction is 6%. Confusing RR value with percentage reduction is a classic boards trap.

q: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has taken metformin 500 mg BID for 4 years. Her CKD has progressed to stage 3b (stable eGFR 35 mL/min/1.73m²), and she has no acute illness. She now requires IV iodinated contrast for a CT scan. Which of the following statements regarding metformin management is correct AND consistent with current ACR (American College of Radiology) guidance?
opts: A. Metformin must be stopped 48 hours before contrast and held for 48 hours after — this applies to all patients receiving iodinated contrast regardless of renal function

B. In patients with eGFR ≥30 mL/min without acute illness, contrast can be administered without withholding metformin — hold metformin at time of contrast and for 48 hours after only if eGFR <30 or acute kidney injury occurs
C. Metformin is absolutely contraindicated below eGFR 30 and must be permanently discontinued before any contrast exposure
D. Lactic acidosis from contrast-metformin interaction occurs through direct nephrotoxicity causing immediate renal failure
exp: The ACR Manual on Contrast Media (2023) divides patients taking metformin into two groups. Group 1 has no AKI and eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73m². These patients do not need to stop metformin either before or after IV iodinated contrast, and renal function does not need to be rechecked afterward. Group 2 has AKI, eGFR <30, or is undergoing arterial catheterization with a high chance of renal artery emboli. These patients should hold metformin at the time of or before the procedure and for 48 hours after, restarting only once renal function is shown to be stable. This patient (stable eGFR 35, no AKI) is in group 1, so metformin can continue. The rationale: contrast-associated AKI is uncommon at eGFR ≥30, and metformin-associated lactic acidosis needs reduced renal clearance. A reflects older, outdated guidance requiring a hold for everyone. C is wrong: metformin is contraindicated at eGFR <30 (FDA label), but the claim that it must be permanently stopped before any contrast exposure is incorrect. D is wrong: contrast does not cause lactic acidosis directly. The risk is indirect, through contrast-associated AKI reducing metformin clearance. Her metformin dose is appropriate (FDA: do not initiate at eGFR 30-45; for continuing patients, reassess and limit to 1,000 mg/day).
ref: Vol 2 Endocrine; ACR Manual on Contrast Media 2020
opts_exp: This reflects older guidance. ACR no longer requires a universal hold, and patients with eGFR 30 or above and no AKI can continue metformin.

Under the ACR Manual on Contrast Media (2023), patients with no AKI and eGFR 30 or above need not stop metformin before or after IV iodinated contrast; holding at the time of contrast and for 48 hours is reserved for AKI, eGFR below 30, or arterial catheterization with a high chance of renal artery emboli. With a stable eGFR of 35 and no AKI, she can continue metformin.
