Metformin is contraindicated at eGFR below 30 per the FDA label, but nothing requires permanent discontinuation before contrast, and her eGFR of 35 is above that threshold.
Contrast does not cause lactic acidosis directly; the risk is indirect, because contrast-associated AKI can reduce metformin clearance and lead to accumulation.

q: A 72-kg man in septic shock (ICU day 3) has bacteremia with Pseudomonas aeruginosa that is resistant to all tested beta-lactams (including ceftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, and cefiderocol), aminoglycosides, and fluoroquinolones. The colistin MIC is 1 mg/L. His creatinine clearance is stable at 45 mL/min. Polymyxin B is unavailable at this institution, so the team selects IV colistimethate (CMS). Per the 2019 International Consensus Guidelines for the polymyxins, which regimen optimizes colistin PK/PD?
opts: A. Colistimethate 2.5 mg/kg/day CBA divided q12h (labeled renal-adjusted dose) with no loading dose
B. Colistimethate loading dose 300 mg CBA (~9 million IU), then 360 mg CBA/day (~11 million IU) divided q12h (normal-renal-function maintenance dose)
C. Colistimethate loading dose 300 mg CBA (~9 million IU), then ~220 mg CBA/day (~6.6 million IU) divided q12h adjusted for CrCl 45 mL/min, starting 12 hours after the load
D. Inhaled colistimethate 1-2 million IU q8-12h as monotherapy to avoid nephrotoxicity
exp: CMS is an inactive prodrug that converts slowly to colistin, so steady-state concentrations take days to reach without a loading dose. The 2019 International Consensus Guidelines (ACCP/ESCMID/IDSA/ISAP/SCCM/SIDP) recommend a loading dose of 300 mg CBA (about 9 million IU; 1 million IU ≈ 33 mg CBA), regardless of renal function. Maintenance starts 12 hours later and is dosed by CrCl because CMS is renally cleared. For CrCl 40-49 mL/min it is about 220 mg CBA/day (3.3 million IU q12h). The target is an average steady-state colistin concentration of about 2 mg/L (free AUC/MIC is the PK/PD index). A is wrong: without a load, therapeutic concentrations are delayed in a patient in septic shock. B is wrong: 360 mg CBA/day is the dose for CrCl ≥90 and would accumulate at CrCl 45, raising nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity risk. D is wrong: inhaled CMS alone does not treat bacteremia. The consensus generally prefers polymyxin B for invasive non-urinary infections because it does not need renal adjustment and reaches target concentrations faster, but that option is unavailable here.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1, Critical Care; Polymyxin pharmacology

q: A 58-year-old patient on ECMO (VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock) requires vancomycin for MRSA bacteremia. Vancomycin is frequently sequestered in ECMO circuits. Which dosing strategy is most appropriate to achieve AUC/MIC 400–600 mg·h/L?
opts: A. Standard weight-based dosing 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h without change
B. Increase empiric loading dose to 35 mg/kg, then daily trough monitoring
C. Use a loading dose of 25-30 mg/kg, then AUC-guided monitoring with Bayesian software
D. Switch to linezolid 600mg q12h (not sequestered by ECMO circuits)
exp: ECMO sequesters vancomycin into the circuit, requiring higher initial loading doses (25-30 mg/kg) to achieve therapeutic concentrations. AUC-guided monitoring using Bayesian pharmacokinetic software is the current standard of care per ASHP/IDSA/SIDP joint guidance. Troughs alone (option B) are no longer recommended. Linezolid (option D) is acceptable for MRSA but the question asks about vancomycin optimization.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; 2020 Vancomycin Therapeutic Monitoring Consensus Guidelines

q: A patient with severe ARDS (P/F ratio 78) fails prone positioning and neuromuscular blockade. The intensivist considers veno-venous ECMO. Which medication dosing concern is MOST unique to VV-ECMO compared to standard ICU care?
opts: A. Increased unbound fentanyl due to hypoalbuminemia
B. Substantial sequestration of lipophilic drugs (fentanyl, midazolam) in ECMO circuit increasing Vd
C. Decreased propofol clearance due to hepatic congestion
D. Heparin dose reduction due to circuit-related antithrombin depletion
exp: VV-ECMO significantly increases the apparent volume of distribution of lipophilic, highly protein-bound drugs such as fentanyl, midazolam, and propofol, because the tubing and oxygenator sequester these agents. This often requires substantially higher doses to achieve adequate sedation/analgesia. Heparin requirements actually often increase (not decrease) due to antithrombin consumption. Hypoalbuminemia affects unbound drug regardless of ECMO.

q: A patient with end-stage renal disease on intermittent HD (4-hour sessions, 3×/week, high-flux membrane) is receiving gentamicin for gram-negative bacteremia, dosed after each dialysis session. To quantify drug removal during dialysis, a gentamicin level drawn at the start of an HD session is 6 mg/L and a level drawn at the end of the 4-hour session is 3 mg/L (assume first-order elimination during HD and ignore post-dialysis rebound). What is the elimination rate constant (ke) during dialysis?
exp: ke = (ln C1 - ln C2) / (t2 - t1) = ln(6/3) / 4 h = 0.693 / 4 = 0.173 h⁻¹. The intradialytic half-life is 0.693 / 0.173 = 4 hours, which fits high-flux HD removing about 50% of gentamicin per 4-hour session. Between sessions, the half-life in ESRD is roughly 30-60 hours, which is why gentamicin is dosed after each dialysis. Distractors: 0.058 h⁻¹ = 0.693/12 (half-life 12 h); 0.116 h⁻¹ = 0.693/6 (half-life 6 h); 0.231 h⁻¹ = 0.693/3 (half-life 3 h).
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Pharmacokinetics; Aminoglycoside kinetics in dialysis

q: A 70-year-old woman (50 kg, SCr 1.2 mg/dL) is on phenytoin 300 mg/day with a total level of 12 mg/L. She is started on valproic acid 500 mg BID. After 2 weeks, total phenytoin is 8 mg/L, but she develops phenytoin toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia). What best explains this paradox?
opts: A. Valproic acid inhibits CYP2C9, increasing phenytoin free fraction despite lower total level
B. Valproic acid only displaces phenytoin from albumin; displacement alone produces a sustained rise in unbound phenytoin concentration at steady state
C. Both displacement from albumin AND CYP2C9 inhibition occur simultaneously
D. Valproic acid induces UGT enzymes, increasing phenytoin glucuronidation
exp: Valproate interacts with phenytoin in two ways. (1) It displaces phenytoin from albumin, raising the free fraction. For a low-extraction, restrictively cleared drug like phenytoin, the higher free fraction increases clearance of total drug, so the total concentration falls (12 to 8 mg/L). At steady state, displacement alone returns the unbound concentration to baseline (unbound Css = dosing rate / intrinsic clearance), so by itself it would not cause sustained toxicity. (2) Valproate also inhibits phenytoin's CYP2C9 (and CYP2C19) metabolism, which lowers intrinsic clearance and raises the unbound concentration. Together they explain a low total level with high free phenytoin and clinical toxicity after 2 weeks. Free phenytoin levels should be monitored during co-therapy. A is wrong: enzyme inhibition does not change the free fraction, and it does not explain the lower total level. B is wrong: displacement alone causes only a transient rise in unbound concentration, not sustained toxicity at steady state. D is wrong: valproate inhibits, rather than induces, glucuronidation, and phenytoin is cleared mainly by CYP2C9 hydroxylation.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; Phenytoin drug interaction pharmacokinetics

q: A patient requires continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) with a CVVHDF effluent rate of 2 L/hr (1 L/hr dialysate + 1 L/hr replacement fluid given post-filter; net ultrafiltration negligible). The sieving coefficient (SC) for meropenem is 0.9. Meropenem Vd = 0.25 L/kg (80 kg patient). What is the estimated meropenem clearance by CRRT?
opts: A. 1.8 L/hr (30 mL/min)
B. 2.0 L/hr (33 mL/min)
C. 0.9 L/hr (15 mL/min)
D. 3.6 L/hr (60 mL/min)
exp: With post-filter replacement, CRRT clearance ≈ SC (or saturation coefficient) × effluent rate. For CVVHDF, effluent = dialysate + replacement (+ net UF) = 1 + 1 = 2 L/hr. CL_CRRT = 0.9 × 2 L/hr = 1.8 L/hr = 1,800 mL / 60 min = 30 mL/min. No predilution correction is needed because replacement is given post-filter; with pre-filter replacement, clearance would be multiplied by Qp/(Qp + Qrep), which needs the blood flow rate. Vd is not needed for clearance. 2.0 L/hr ignores the SC, 0.9 L/hr counts only one fluid stream, and 3.6 L/hr double-counts the effluent. This CRRT clearance supports meropenem doses of about 1 g q8h (or 500 mg q6h) at this effluent rate for MICs ≤2 mg/L.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, CRRT pharmacokinetics; Drug dosing in renal replacement therapy

q: A patient receives a two-compartment drug IV bolus. The plasma concentration vs time curve shows a biexponential decay: C(t) = 10e⁻⁰·⁶ᵗ + 4e⁻⁰·¹ᵗ (mg/L; t in hours). What is the AUC₀→∞?
opts: A. 14 mg·h/L
B. 56.7 mg·h/L
C. 6.4 mg·h/L
D. 140 mg·h/L
exp: For a biexponential curve C(t) = A·e^(−αt) + B·e^(−βt), AUC₀→∞ = A/α + B/β = 10/0.6 + 4/0.1 = 16.67 + 40 = 56.7 mg·h/L. A (14) is just the sum of the intercepts (C0), not an area. C (6.4) multiplies instead of divides (10×0.6 + 4×0.1). D (140) divides the total intercept by β alone (14/0.1), which ignores the faster distribution phase. Clearance can then be calculated as CL = Dose/AUC.

q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 210 cells/µL, VL 88,000 copies/mL) is starting ART. He has HLA-B*5701 positive result. Which ART component must be AVOIDED and why?
opts: A. Tenofovir DF — risk of nephrotoxicity is HLA-linked
B. Abacavir — HLA-B*5701 positivity predicts hypersensitivity syndrome (HSR)
C. Efavirenz — HLA-B*5701 predicts CNS toxicity
D. Dolutegravir — neural tube defect risk increases with HLA-B*5701
exp: HLA-B*5701 allele positivity predicts a severe, potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction to abacavir (ABC), a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor. Screening for HLA-B*5701 before prescribing abacavir is recommended by DHHS guidelines; if positive, abacavir is absolutely contraindicated. The other drugs listed are not HLA-B*5701 linked.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1, HIV pharmacotherapy; DHHS ART Guidelines

q: A 62-year-old liver transplant recipient on tacrolimus (trough 7 ng/mL) develops a Candida krusei fungemia. Which antifungal is most appropriate?
opts: A. Fluconazole 800mg load then 400mg daily — broadest oral bioavailability
B. Echinocandin (micafungin 100mg daily) — intrinsic fluconazole resistance
C. Voriconazole 6mg/kg q12h x2 then 4mg/kg q12h — broadest spectrum
D. Amphotericin B liposomal 3-5mg/kg/day — avoid all azoles in transplant
exp: Candida krusei is INTRINSICALLY resistant to fluconazole. Echinocandins (micafungin, caspofungin, anidulafungin) are first-line for Candida krusei fungemia per IDSA guidelines. Voriconazole has activity against C. krusei but is not first-line and has significant drug interactions with tacrolimus (CYP3A4 inhibition → tacrolimus toxicity). Liposomal amphotericin B is an alternative but more toxic.

q: A patient is admitted to the ICU with septic shock from a urinary source and remains on norepinephrine. Serum albumin is 1.9 g/dL. Blood cultures grow ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae that is ceftriaxone-resistant, susceptible to ertapenem and meropenem (both MIC ≤0.5 mg/L), and susceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam. She received one dose of ceftriaxone in the ED. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
opts: A. Continue ceftriaxone — she received it in the ED and is being resuscitated
B. Ertapenem 1 g IV q24h — once-daily carbapenem active against ESBL-E
C. Meropenem 1 g IV q8h
D. Ceftazidime-avibactam — spares carbapenem use
exp: Carbapenems are the treatment of choice for serious ESBL-producing Enterobacterales infections. The IDSA AMR Guidance (2023/2024) states that for critically ill and/or hypoalbuminemic patients, meropenem or imipenem-cilastatin is preferred over ertapenem. Ertapenem is about 85-95% protein bound, so in hypoalbuminemia its free fraction and clearance rise and target attainment falls. Its once-daily dosing also gives little margin in septic shock. This patient is on vasopressors with albumin 1.9 g/dL, so meropenem is preferred. Once she stabilizes, de-escalation to ertapenem or an oral agent (TMP-SMX or a fluoroquinolone if susceptible) is reasonable. A is wrong: the isolate is ceftriaxone-resistant (the IDSA definition of ESBL-E for practical purposes), and the MERINO trial showed even piperacillin-tazobactam was inferior to meropenem for ESBL bloodstream infection. B is reasonable for stable patients but not preferred in critical illness with hypoalbuminemia. D is wrong: IDSA advises reserving ceftazidime-avibactam for carbapenem-resistant organisms (e.g., KPC) to preserve its activity.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; IDSA Guidance for ESBL Enterobacterales 2022

q: A patient with HIV (CD4 45 cells/µL, on prophylaxis with TMP-SMX) develops cryptococcal meningitis confirmed by CSF India ink and cryptococcal antigen. LP opening pressure is 42 cmH₂O. Which initial treatment plan is MOST appropriate?
opts: A. Fluconazole 800mg/day x2 weeks then 400mg/day consolidation
B. Liposomal amphotericin B 3-4mg/kg/day + flucytosine 25mg/kg q6h x2 weeks; serial therapeutic LPs
C. Amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7-1mg/kg/day + fluconazole 400mg/day x2 weeks
D. Voriconazole 4mg/kg q12h (cryptococcal CSF penetration >90%)
exp: For HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, the IDSA 2010 cryptococcal guideline and the US DHHS Adult/Adolescent OI Guidelines recommend induction with liposomal amphotericin B 3-4 mg/kg/day plus flucytosine 25 mg/kg q6h (100 mg/kg/day) for at least 2 weeks. This is followed by fluconazole 400-800 mg/day consolidation for at least 8 weeks, then maintenance. An opening pressure ≥25 cmH₂O with symptoms calls for daily therapeutic LPs (remove CSF to halve the pressure or bring it below 20 cmH₂O) until stable. Raised intracranial pressure is a leading cause of early death. ART is delayed about 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS risk. A is wrong: fluconazole monotherapy induction is inferior, with slower CSF clearance and higher mortality. C is wrong: amphotericin B deoxycholate plus fluconazole is an alternative only when flucytosine is unavailable, it uses fluconazole 800 mg/day (not 400), and deoxycholate is more nephrotoxic. D is wrong: voriconazole has no role in induction, and its CSF penetration is about 50%, not >90%. WHO 2022 prefers a single dose of liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg plus 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole 1,200 mg/day, mainly for resource-limited settings. US guidance still supports option B.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; IDSA 2010 Cryptococcal Meningitis Guidelines

q: A 68-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 22%, NYHA class II-III), CKD Stage 3b (eGFR 32), and potassium 5.3 mEq/L is on sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg BID, metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily, and eplerenone 25 mg daily. He is in sinus rhythm with a resting HR of 62 bpm and BP of 108/70. His NT-proBNP is 4800 pg/mL. What next step optimizes guideline-directed therapy?
opts: A. Add ivabradine — further reduces HF hospitalization in sinus rhythm
B. Increase eplerenone to 50 mg — MRA dose titration improves outcomes
C. Add an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin 10 mg or empagliflozin 10 mg daily) and continue eplerenone with close potassium monitoring
D. Start hydralazine-isosorbide dinitrate — additional vasodilation with ARNI
exp: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline lists four foundational HFrEF therapies: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, an evidence-based beta-blocker, an MRA, and an SGLT2 inhibitor (each Class 1). He is missing the SGLT2 inhibitor. Dapagliflozin (eGFR ≥25) and empagliflozin (eGFR ≥20) can be started at eGFR 32 (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced). SGLT2 inhibitors may also reduce hyperkalemia risk and help keep the MRA on board. Eplerenone should continue: the MRA is held only when K >5.5 or eGFR <30, and K 5.3 calls for closer monitoring, not discontinuation. A is wrong: ivabradine (SHIFT) requires sinus rhythm with resting HR ≥70 bpm on a maximally tolerated beta-blocker, and his HR is 62. B is wrong: with eGFR 30-49 the eplerenone maximum is 25 mg daily, and K is already 5.3. D is wrong: hydralazine-ISDN is recommended for self-identified African American patients with NYHA III-IV symptoms despite optimal GDMT (A-HeFT), or for those who cannot take an ARNI/ACEi/ARB. Neither applies, and BP of 108/70 leaves little room.

q: A patient undergoes PCI with a drug-eluting stent for NSTEMI and receives ticagrelor 90 mg BID + aspirin 81 mg. Six months post-PCI, she needs hip replacement surgery. Orthopedics and cardiology agree the surgery cannot be safely deferred (progressive femoral head collapse with loss of ambulation), and the surgeon cannot operate on full DAPT. What is the best perioperative antiplatelet plan?
opts: A. Switch to clopidogrel 5 days pre-op (less bleeding, maintains P2Y12 inhibition)
B. Continue ticagrelor through surgery — bleeding risk acceptable for major orthopedic surgery
C. Stop ticagrelor 3-5 days pre-op (vs 5 days for clopidogrel), continue aspirin, and restart ticagrelor within 24-48 h post-op once hemostasis is secure
D. Switch to IV cangrelor as a bridge for the 3 days before surgery
exp: When possible, elective noncardiac surgery should be deferred until the planned DAPT course after ACS-PCI is complete. Here the team has decided surgery cannot wait. The 2024 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline (and the 2016 ACC/AHA DAPT focused update) then recommends continuing aspirin through surgery unless bleeding risk is prohibitive, such as some neurosurgical or spinal procedures. The P2Y12 inhibitor is stopped for the shortest interval: ticagrelor 3-5 days, clopidogrel 5 days, prasugrel 7 days. It is restarted, ideally with a loading dose, within 24-48 hours once surgical hemostasis allows. A is wrong: switching to clopidogrel still requires a 5-day hold, so it adds no protection and is a less effective agent after ACS. B is wrong: continuing a potent P2Y12 inhibitor through major orthopedic surgery carries high bleeding risk, which the surgeon has already ruled out. D is wrong: cangrelor bridging is off-label and is considered only for very high thrombotic risk, such as stent placement within about the prior month. It is not needed 6 months after PCI.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; ACC/AHA Perioperative DAPT Guidance

q: A patient with mechanical mitral valve (bileaflet) is on warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5). She develops INR 9.2 with minor bruising and gingival bleeding but no major hemorrhage. She had a supratherapeutic INR because her provider started clarithromycin. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: A. Hold warfarin, administer vitamin K 10mg IV for rapid reversal
B. Hold warfarin, administer oral vitamin K 1-2.5mg, recheck INR in 24-48 hours
C. Hold warfarin only — INR will self-correct within 3-5 days
D. Administer 4F-PCC and vitamin K 10mg IV for immediate reversal
exp: For INR >8 with minor bleeding in a mechanical valve patient: Hold warfarin and administer LOW-dose oral vitamin K (1-2.5mg) to gently lower INR without over-correcting. Over-correction (high-dose IV vitamin K) risks thrombosis of the mechanical valve. 4F-PCC is reserved for life-threatening bleeding. Holding alone (option C) is too slow given INR 9.2. Oral vitamin K 1-2.5mg provides controlled reversal within 24-48h.

q: A 78-year-old male with AF and CrCl 19 mL/min (Cockcroft-Gault) is currently on apixaban 5mg BID. His cardiologist orders a renal panel: SCr 3.4 mg/dL, age 78, weight 62 kg. Which dose adjustment is correct per FDA labeling for apixaban?
opts: A. No change needed — apixaban dose adjustment criteria use TWO of three (age ≥80, SCr ≥1.5, weight ≤60 kg)
B. Reduce to apixaban 2.5mg BID — CrCl <25 mL/min triggers automatic dose reduction
C. Discontinue apixaban; ESRD patients require warfarin only
D. Reduce to apixaban 2.5 mg BID because 2 reduction criteria are met (SCr ≥1.5 mg/dL and CrCl <25 mL/min)
exp: Per the FDA apixaban label for nonvalvular AF, the dose is reduced to 2.5 mg BID only when at least 2 of these 3 are present: age ≥80 years, weight ≤60 kg, SCr ≥1.5 mg/dL. This patient meets only one (SCr 3.4). He is 78 and weighs 62 kg, so 5 mg BID continues. CrCl is not one of the apixaban criteria, and the label does not reduce the dose for CrCl alone, even in ESRD on dialysis unless age or weight criteria are met. Patients with CrCl <25 mL/min were excluded from ARISTOTLE, so close monitoring is reasonable. B and D are wrong because CrCl is not a dose-reduction criterion for apixaban (it is used for rivaroxaban, edoxaban, and dabigatran). C is wrong: CrCl 19 mL/min is not ESRD, and the label allows apixaban even in ESRD on hemodialysis.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; Apixaban prescribing information; DOAC renal dosing

q: A 52-year-old woman with T2DM and HFrEF (EF 35%) presents with A1c 9.2%. She is on metformin 1000mg BID, sitagliptin 100mg daily. eGFR is 52 mL/min/1.73m². What addition best addresses both glucose control AND her cardiovascular/HF risk?
opts: A. Liraglutide 1.8mg SC daily — LEADER trial mortality benefit in T2DM + CVD
B. Empagliflozin 10mg daily — reduced CV death and HF hospitalization in T2DM (EMPA-REG OUTCOME) and the composite of CV death or HF hospitalization in HFrEF (EMPEROR-Reduced)
C. Insulin glargine 0.2 U/kg/day — provides better A1c reduction than oral agents
D. Pioglitazone 30mg daily — improves insulin sensitivity and reduces MACE
exp: Empagliflozin is the only option that addresses both glucose and HF risk. In EMPA-REG OUTCOME (T2DM with ASCVD) it lowered CV death, all-cause death, and HF hospitalization. In EMPEROR-Reduced (HFrEF with or without diabetes) it lowered the primary composite of CV death or HF hospitalization, driven mainly by fewer HF hospitalizations. It is FDA-approved for HF regardless of diabetes status, can be used at eGFR 52, and gives modest A1c lowering. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline and ADA Standards of Care 2024 recommend an SGLT2 inhibitor in T2DM with HF. A is wrong: LEADER showed MACE and mortality benefit in T2DM with high CV risk but no HF benefit. Liraglutide was neutral, with a trend toward harm, in advanced HFrEF (FIGHT) and increased heart rate and cardiac events in LIVE, so it is not the choice for HF risk. C is wrong: insulin lowers A1c but has no CV or HF benefit and causes weight gain and hypoglycemia. D is wrong: pioglitazone causes fluid retention, has a boxed warning for HF, and is contraindicated in NYHA III-IV HF.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Endocrine; ADA Standards of Medical Care 2024; EMPEROR-Reduced

q: A patient with type 1 diabetes on insulin pump therapy presents with DKA (pH 7.18, glucose 520 mg/dL, bicarb 10 mEq/L, anion gap 28). Potassium is 3.2 mEq/L. What is the correct insulin and potassium management?
opts: A. Start insulin drip immediately at 0.1 U/kg/hr; add KCl to fluids once K+ is below 5.3
B. Hold insulin drip until potassium ≥3.3 mEq/L; replace K+ aggressively first (20-30 mEq/hr), then start insulin
C. Start insulin at 0.1 U/kg/hr AND give KCl 20-30 mEq/hr simultaneously given hypokalemia
D. Use subcutaneous insulin correction doses since pump failure likely caused DKA
exp: Insulin moves potassium into cells, so starting insulin when K is already low can cause life-threatening hypokalemia and arrhythmias. If baseline K is below 3.3 mEq/L, insulin is held and IV potassium is given at 20-30 mEq/h until K is at least 3.3. If K is 3.3 to below 5.3, insulin is started and 20-30 mEq of potassium is added to each liter of IV fluid. If K is 5.3 or higher, potassium is held and monitored. With K 3.2 mEq/L, insulin must wait. A is wrong: it starts insulin immediately despite hypokalemia. C is wrong: starting insulin while K is below 3.3, even with replacement running, risks worsening hypokalemia. D is wrong: moderate-to-severe DKA (pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10) is treated with IV fluids and IV insulin once K is corrected; the pump should be stopped, and subcutaneous correction doses are not appropriate initial therapy. Updated after the 2024 course: the 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS hyperglycemic crises consensus raised the insulin-hold threshold to K below 3.5 mEq/L with about 10-20 mEq/h replacement (Diabetes Care, 2024).
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; ADA DKA Management Guidelines
opts_exp: Starting insulin immediately with K 3.2 mEq/L drives potassium into cells and can cause life-threatening hypokalemia; insulin must wait until K is at least 3.3.
With baseline K below 3.3 mEq/L, insulin is held and IV potassium is given at 20-30 mEq/h until K reaches at least 3.3, then the insulin infusion is started.
Giving potassium at the same time does not make it safe to start insulin while K is below 3.3; insulin is held until K is corrected.
Moderate-to-severe DKA needs IV fluids and IV insulin after K is corrected; the pump is stopped, and subcutaneous correction doses are not appropriate initial therapy.

q: A 67-year-old with COPD (GOLD Group E — 3 exacerbations last year, CAT score 28, FEV₁ 38% predicted) is on LABA/LAMA (tiotropium + salmeterol). He also has an eosinophil count of 420 cells/µL. Which treatment modification is supported by evidence to reduce exacerbations?
opts: A. Add roflumilast 500 mcg daily — PDE4 inhibitor reduces exacerbations in chronic bronchitis phenotype
B. Add ICS to form triple therapy (LABA/LAMA/ICS) — IMPACT and ETHOS showed fewer exacerbations, with greater benefit at higher blood eosinophil counts
C. Switch to azithromycin 250mg daily for exacerbation prophylaxis
D. Both A and B are appropriate add-on options with evidence for this patient
exp: GOLD 2024 follow-up pharmacotherapy: for patients who keep exacerbating on LABA/LAMA, escalate to LABA/LAMA/ICS when blood eosinophils are ≥100 cells/µL. Benefit is greatest at ≥300, and this patient has 420. IMPACT and ETHOS showed fewer moderate/severe exacerbations with triple therapy, and ETHOS showed lower all-cause mortality with full-dose budesonide. A and D are wrong: GOLD places roflumilast for patients with FEV1 <50% AND chronic bronchitis, mainly when eosinophils are <100. Chronic bronchitis is not described here, and the high eosinophil count favors ICS. C is wrong: azithromycin is an add-on option (mainly for former smokers with eosinophils <100), not a replacement for bronchodilators, and switching would remove LABA/LAMA. Updated after the 2024 course: GOLD 2025 added dupilumab for patients on triple therapy with eosinophils ≥300 and chronic bronchitis, and ensifentrine as a maintenance option; the answer is unchanged.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Pulmonology; GOLD 2024 Report; IMPACT trial
opts_exp: GOLD reserves roflumilast for patients with FEV1 below 50% and chronic bronchitis, mainly when eosinophils are below 100 cells/µL. Chronic bronchitis is not described here, and an eosinophil count of 420 favors ICS.

GOLD 2024 recommends escalating to LABA/LAMA/ICS for patients who keep exacerbating on LABA/LAMA with eosinophils of 100 cells/µL or more, with the greatest benefit at 300 or more; he has 420. IMPACT and ETHOS showed fewer moderate or severe exacerbations with triple therapy, and ETHOS showed lower all-cause mortality with full-dose budesonide.
Azithromycin is an add-on option, mainly for former smokers with eosinophils below 100, not a replacement for bronchodilators; switching would remove his LABA/LAMA.
Only ICS escalation is supported by this patient's eosinophil count; the chronic bronchitis phenotype needed for roflumilast is not established.
reviewNote: Targeted correction 2026-10-19; full chapter review pending.

q: A 44-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO Group 1, WHO FC III) and is treatment-naive. She has no cardiopulmonary comorbidities or contraindications. Her 6-minute walk distance is 380 m, NT-proBNP is 700 ng/L, and echocardiography shows a right atrial area of 20 cm² without pericardial effusion; she has no syncope. By the ESC/ERS 2022 risk assessment she is intermediate risk. What initial therapy is recommended for this risk level?
opts: A. Sildenafil monotherapy — first-line for WHO FC III PAH
B. Ambrisentan + tadalafil (AMBITION trial) — upfront combination has superior outcomes vs monotherapy
C. IV epoprostenol + bosentan — only option for severe FC III disease
D. Subcutaneous treprostinil + sildenafil — parenteral prostacyclin required for FC III
exp: In ESC/ERS 2022, a 6MWD of 165-440 m, NT-proBNP of 300-1,100 ng/L, and an RA area of 18-26 cm² all place her at intermediate risk. For treatment-naive PAH patients without cardiopulmonary comorbidities at low or intermediate risk, ESC/ERS 2022 recommends initial dual oral therapy with an ERA plus a PDE5 inhibitor (Class I). CHEST 2019 likewise recommends ambrisentan plus tadalafil for treatment-naive FC II-III patients. In AMBITION, upfront ambrisentan plus tadalafil reduced clinical failure by about 50% compared with pooled monotherapy. A is wrong: monotherapy is reserved for selected patients (e.g., with cardiopulmonary comorbidities or vasoreactive disease). C and D are wrong: initial therapy that includes IV/SC prostacyclin is recommended for high-risk patients (e.g., FC IV, 6MWD <165 m, NT-proBNP >1,100 ng/L, RA area >26 cm², pericardial effusion), not intermediate risk. Parenteral prostacyclin is not required for FC III, and neither regimen is the 'only option'.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; AMBITION Trial; 2022 ESC/ERS PAH Guidelines

q: A 58-year-old woman with CKD Stage 4 (eGFR 28) and type 2 diabetes has albumin-to-creatinine ratio 1,800 mg/g on maximal ACE inhibitor therapy (lisinopril 40mg/day, K+ 4.8 mEq/L). She is not on an MRA or SGLT2 inhibitor. Blood pressure is 138/88 despite 3 antihypertensives. Which addition(s) to her regimen are best supported to slow CKD progression?
opts: A. Spironolactone 25mg daily — MRA provides additional proteinuria reduction
B. Finerenone 10-20mg daily — nonsteroidal MRA reduces CKD progression and CV events in T2DM with CKD (FIDELIO-DKD)
C. Empagliflozin 10mg daily — EMPA-KIDNEY showed reduced kidney disease progression or CV death (consistent with CREDENCE and DAPA-CKD for other SGLT2 inhibitors)
D. Both B and C are recommended; evidence supports combination in CKD + T2DM
exp: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD and ADA Standards of Care 2024 recommend layered therapy. First, an SGLT2 inhibitor for T2DM with eGFR ≥20 (1A); empagliflozin in EMPA-KIDNEY, canagliflozin in CREDENCE, and dapagliflozin in DAPA-CKD all slowed kidney disease progression independent of glucose lowering. Second, finerenone for persistent albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g) despite maximal RAS blockade, with eGFR ≥25 and K ≤5.0 (2A; FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD). Finerenone starts at 10 mg daily when eGFR is 25-<60 and is titrated to 20 mg if K ≤4.8. With eGFR 28, K 4.8, and ACR 1,800 mg/g on maximal ACEi, she qualifies for both. B and C are each correct but incomplete. A is wrong: spironolactone lowers albuminuria but has no kidney or CV outcome data in diabetic CKD and carries more hyperkalemia risk at eGFR 28. Updated after the 2024 course: the CONFIDENCE trial (NEJM 2025) showed that starting finerenone and empagliflozin together lowered UACR more than either alone, supporting the combination.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Nephrology; KDIGO 2022 CKD Guidelines; FIDELIO-DKD

q: A 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder becomes pregnant (6 weeks). She is on lithium 900mg/day (level 0.8 mEq/L) and lamotrigine 200mg/day. Which medication management is most appropriate given the teratogenicity profile?
opts: A. Discontinue lithium immediately — Ebstein anomaly risk is absolute contraindication in pregnancy

B. Continue both medications with fetal echocardiography and close level monitoring; the absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly/right ventricular outflow tract defects with first-trimester lithium is low (about 0.6% vs 0.2% unexposed), and benefit-risk favors continuation
C. Switch lithium to valproate — better evidence in bipolar I during pregnancy
D. Discontinue both medications — all mood stabilizers are category D or X in pregnancy
exp: Lithium raises the relative risk of cardiac malformations, but the absolute risk is low. In the largest cohort (Patorno, NEJM 2017; about 1.3 million pregnancies), cardiac malformations occurred in 2.4% of lithium-exposed vs 1.2% of unexposed infants. Right ventricular outflow tract defects, including Ebstein anomaly, occurred in 0.6% vs 0.2%, with higher risk at doses >900 mg/day. Older estimates of 1 in 1,000 versus 1 in 20,000 for Ebstein anomaly came from smaller studies. Stopping lithium abruptly sharply raises relapse risk, and maternal mood episodes carry serious risks (suicide, poor prenatal care, postpartum psychosis). For a patient with bipolar I who is stable on lithium, ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline 5 (2023) supports shared decision-making that often favors continuation. Use the lowest effective dose in divided doses, monitor levels frequently (clearance rises in pregnancy), get a fetal echocardiogram at about 18-22 weeks, and plan delivery-related dose adjustments. Lamotrigine has reassuring pregnancy data and can continue, with levels monitored because clearance rises. A is wrong: lithium is not absolutely contraindicated, and abrupt withdrawal is harmful. C is wrong: valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the mood stabilizers (about 10% major malformations, neural tube defects, lower IQ, autism) and should be avoided in pregnancy. D is wrong: FDA letter categories were removed by the 2015 PLLR, and stopping all therapy risks relapse.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1, Psychiatry; ACOG Bipolar Disorder in Pregnancy Guidelines

q: A 32-year-old male with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has failed 3 adequate antipsychotic trials. Clozapine 300mg/day is initiated. Week 4 ANC is 1,200 cells/mm³ (down from 4,800 baseline). What is the appropriate action per REMS guidelines?
opts: A. Continue clozapine — mild neutropenia; monitor ANC three times weekly until ≥1,500/mm³
B. Reduce clozapine dose by 50% and recheck ANC in 3 days
C. Interrupt clozapine; ANC <1,500 triggers hold; recheck ANC every day until ≥1,500, then every week x4 weeks
D. Permanently discontinue clozapine; ANC <1,500 is an absolute contraindication to re-challenge
exp: Clozapine labeling and the Clozapine REMS ANC algorithm for the general population define three levels. Mild neutropenia (ANC 1,000-1,499/mm³): continue clozapine and monitor ANC three times weekly until ≥1,500, then return to the previous monitoring interval. Moderate (500-999): interrupt, check ANC daily until ≥1,000, then three times weekly until ≥1,500, and rechallenge may be considered. Severe (<500): stop, and generally do not rechallenge. ANC 1,200 is mild neutropenia, so clozapine continues with three-times-weekly ANC (A). B is wrong: dose reduction is not part of the algorithm. C is wrong: interruption applies at ANC <1,000, not <1,500. D is wrong: permanent discontinuation applies to severe neutropenia (<500). Updated after the 2024 course: FDA eliminated the Clozapine REMS in February 2025; the ANC monitoring recommendations remain in labeling.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; FDA Clozapine REMS Guidelines 2021

q: A 34-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting MS (2 relapses/year, 5 new T2 lesions) is on interferon beta-1a and wants to switch to a higher-efficacy agent. She plans pregnancy in 2 years, strongly prefers an oral medication given as short courses rather than regular infusions, and wants no ongoing drug exposure when she tries to conceive. Which agent best fits her goals with an acceptable reproductive safety profile?
opts: A. Natalizumab — high efficacy, but PML risk and must stop ≥3 months before conception
B. Alemtuzumab — durable remission after 2 IV treatment courses; contraception for 4 months after each course
C. Ocrelizumab — IV B-cell depletion every 6 months; label advises contraception for 6 months after the last infusion
D. Cladribine — oral, high efficacy, two short annual treatment courses; contraception required during each course and for 6 months after the last dose of each course
exp: Cladribine tablets are the only oral, short-course, high-efficacy option offered. Two yearly courses of 4-5 tablet days per month for 2 months give durable efficacy (CLARITY) without continuous dosing. Per the label, pregnancy must be excluded before each course, and contraception is required during each course and for 6 months after its last dose. Pregnancy can then be planned with no ongoing drug exposure, which fits her 2-year timeline. A is wrong for her goals: natalizumab is a monthly infusion with PML risk. The label sets no fixed washout, but stopping it before conception risks rebound disease, so it is often continued into pregnancy. B is wrong for her goals: alemtuzumab is IV and carries secondary autoimmunity (thyroid disease, ITP, nephropathy) requiring 4 years of monthly monitoring, including during pregnancy. C is wrong for her goals: ocrelizumab is an ongoing IV therapy. Anti-CD20 therapy is a reasonable pregnancy-planning option for patients willing to receive infusions, but it does not meet her stated preference.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1, Neurology; EAN/ECTRIMS MS Pregnancy Guidelines

q: A 72-year-old male with acute ischemic stroke (NIHSS 18, large vessel occlusion) receives IV alteplase at 2.5 hours and undergoes thrombectomy at 4.8 hours. His blood pressure is 210/115 mmHg post-thrombolysis. What is the BP target and optimal agent?
opts: A. Target <180/105 mmHg using IV labetalol or nicardipine; avoid excessive lowering
B. Target <160/90 mmHg aggressively — reduces hemorrhagic transformation risk
C. No BP treatment needed — autoregulation maintains perfusion in penumbra
D. Target MAP <130 mmHg using IV clevidipine — most titratable option
exp: Post-IV thrombolysis, the BP target is <180/105 mmHg per AHA/ASA stroke guidelines. More aggressive lowering risks hypoperfusion of the ischemic penumbra. First-line agents: IV labetalol (10-20mg over 1-2 min; max 300mg) or IV nicardipine (5-15 mg/hr continuous infusion). Clevidipine is also acceptable but not specifically preferred over nicardipine. Nitroprusside/nitrates should be avoided (cerebral vasodilation increases ICP).

q: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer progresses on pertuzumab + trastuzumab + docetaxel after 8 cycles. ECOG PS 1. What second-line therapy has the strongest overall survival evidence?
opts: A. Lapatinib + capecitabine (EGF100151 trial)
B. Trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1/ado-trastuzumab emtansine) — EMILIA trial OS benefit
C. Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) — DESTINY-Breast03 showed superior PFS and OS vs T-DM1
D. Neratinib + capecitabine — NALA trial benefit
exp: In DESTINY-Breast03 (HER2+ mBC previously treated with trastuzumab and a taxane), T-DXd beat T-DM1 head to head. PFS was 28.8 vs 6.8 months (HR 0.33), and overall survival was significantly longer (HR 0.64; Hurvitz, Lancet 2023). Because it improved OS over the prior standard, T-DXd has the strongest OS evidence and is the NCCN-preferred second-line therapy after THP. ILD/pneumonitis occurred in about 15% of patients in DESTINY-Breast03 (mostly grade 1-2), so it needs monitoring. B: EMILIA showed an OS benefit of T-DM1 over lapatinib-capecitabine, but T-DM1 was then shown to be inferior to T-DXd and has moved to later lines. A: EGF100151 improved time to progression, but OS was not significantly improved. D: NALA improved PFS compared with lapatinib-capecitabine, but the OS difference was not significant.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Oncology; DESTINY-Breast03; NCCN Breast Cancer v2.2024

q: A 65-year-old male receives CHOP-R (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) for DLBCL. After cycle 2, he develops numbness and tingling in fingers/toes, bilateral foot drop. Vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy (VIPN) is suspected. What management is appropriate?
opts: A. Add gabapentin for symptomatic relief; continue vincristine at full dose
B. Delay next cycle until resolution, then reduce vincristine dose by 50%
C. Omit vincristine from next cycle; VIPN with foot drop is motor neuropathy indicating dose discontinuation
D. Switch entire regimen to DA-EPOCH-R which uses continuous vincristine infusion to reduce VIPN
exp: Vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy (VIPN) grading guides management: Motor neuropathy (foot drop = Grade 3-4) is an indication to discontinue vincristine. Foot drop/functional impairment is a Grade 3+ motor toxicity requiring omission of vincristine from subsequent cycles per NCCN and institutional guidelines. Dose reduction alone is insufficient for motor neuropathy with functional loss. DA-EPOCH-R uses continuous infusion vincristine but switching regimens at this point is not indicated.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; NCCN B-cell Lymphomas; Vincristine toxicity management

q: An 84-year-old male with moderate dementia, HTN, AF, CKD 3 (CrCl 38), and insomnia is brought by family who report new confusion. His medications include lisinopril, metoprolol, apixaban 2.5mg BID, diphenhydramine 50mg nightly (OTC), and donepezil 10mg. What is the most likely cause of his worsening confusion and appropriate change?
opts: A. Donepezil causing cholinergic excess — reduce dose to 5mg
B. Apixaban causing microhemorrhages — hold and order brain MRI
C. Diphenhydramine (Beers Criteria) — anticholinergic effect worsens dementia/cognition; discontinue immediately
D. Metoprolol causing CNS depression in the elderly — switch to carvedilol
exp: Diphenhydramine is on the Beers Criteria as a 'strong anticholinergic' agent that is explicitly contraindicated in older adults — especially those with dementia, where it markedly worsens cognition, causes confusion, hallucinations, falls, and urinary retention. Anticholinergic burden is a well-established risk in geriatric patients with dementia. Donepezil (cholinesterase inhibitor) would counteract anticholinergic effects. The first intervention should be immediate discontinuation of diphenhydramine. Alternatives: melatonin, low-dose doxepin, or CBT-I.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Geriatrics; AGS 2023 Beers Criteria

q: A 4-year-old child (18 kg) presents with acute status epilepticus. Seizure has been continuous for 8 minutes. IV access is unavailable. What is the first-line treatment?
opts: A. Rectal diazepam 0.2 mg/kg — established non-IV option when IV access is unavailable
B. Intranasal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg total, ≤5 mg per nostril) — effective non-IV first-line benzodiazepine with rapid onset
C. IM lorazepam 0.05 mg/kg — reliable absorption; preferred per pediatric guidelines
D. Buccal midazolam 0.05 mg/kg — established non-IV benzodiazepine for pediatric SE
exp: The AES 2016 status epilepticus guideline recommends a benzodiazepine once a seizure lasts ≥5 minutes. When there is no IV access, options are IM midazolam (Level A), intranasal or buccal midazolam, or rectal diazepam (Level B), each at the correct dose. Intranasal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (3.6 mg for 18 kg; max 10 mg total, split between nostrils) is correctly dosed. It has rapid onset and efficacy comparable to IV diazepam, and it controlled seizures faster than rectal diazepam in pediatric trials. A is wrong: 0.2 mg/kg is the rectal diazepam dose for age ≥12 years. A 4-year-old (age 2-5) needs 0.5 mg/kg (about 9-10 mg), so 0.2 mg/kg is subtherapeutic. C is wrong: IM lorazepam is absorbed slowly and erratically, and guidelines do not recommend it. IM midazolam is the IM benzodiazepine of choice (RAMPART). D is wrong: buccal midazolam is dosed at about 0.3-0.5 mg/kg (max 10 mg), so 0.05 mg/kg (0.9 mg) is a tenfold underdose.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Pediatrics; Pediatric SE Management Guidelines

q: A 52-year-old man with cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) and large ascites presents with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) confirmed by PMN count >250/mm³ in peritoneal fluid. What is the correct treatment including prevention of hepatorenal syndrome?
opts: A. Cefotaxime 2g IV q8h alone — adequate antibiotic coverage for SBP
B. Cefotaxime 2g IV q8h + albumin 1.5 g/kg IV on Day 1 and 1.0 g/kg on Day 3 — albumin prevents HRS
C. Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h + albumin 1.5 g/kg IV — quinolone equally effective as cephalosporin
D. Ceftriaxone 1g IV q24h alone — sufficient for outpatient treatment of mild SBP
exp: SBP treatment: Cefotaxime 2g IV q8h (or ceftriaxone 1g q24h) is first-line antibiotic. The key additional intervention is albumin infusion — IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on Day 1 + 1.0 g/kg on Day 3 — proven in the Sort et al. NEJM 1999 trial to significantly reduce the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) and mortality in SBP patients with SCr >1 mg/dL, BUN >30 mg/dL, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL. This is a guideline-recommended standard of care. SBP is not appropriate for outpatient management in Child-Pugh B/C patients.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, GI; AASLD SBP Guidelines; Sort et al. NEJM 1999

q: A 44-year-old woman with Crohn's disease (perianal fistulizing, on azathioprine) has active disease despite 3 months of therapy. Infliximab is planned. Before initiation, which screening tests are MOST critical?
opts: A. CBC with differential and LFTs only — monitor for azathioprine toxicity
B. TB screening (IGRA or TST), hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), and review vaccinations (give inactivated vaccines; live vaccines generally avoided while on azathioprine)
C. TB screening, hepatitis C antibody, and HIV test
D. Only IGRA for TB — other infections are not significantly reactivated by TNF inhibitors
exp: Before starting infliximab: (1) screen for latent TB with an IGRA or TST and treat latent TB before starting, since infliximab's boxed warning covers serious infections including TB. (2) Check hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), because TNF inhibitors can reactivate HBV (a labeled warning); vaccinate non-immune patients and give antiviral prophylaxis to HBsAg-positive patients. (3) Update vaccinations. Inactivated vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, recombinant zoster, HBV) can be given. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) should be given at least 4 weeks before immunosuppression, so they are generally avoided in this patient who is already on azathioprine. ACG 2018 Crohn's guideline and IDSA 2013 vaccination guidance support this. A is wrong: it misses the infection screening required before anti-TNF therapy. C is wrong: HCV and HIV screening are reasonable but it omits HBV, the most important viral reactivation risk. D is wrong: HBV, invasive fungal, and other opportunistic infections are well-documented risks with TNF inhibitors.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; ACG Crohn's Disease Guidelines; TNFi pre-screening

q: A randomized trial of a new antibiotic vs placebo reports: OR 2.4 (95% CI 1.1–5.2, p=0.03) for clinical cure. An accompanying meta-analysis shows OR 1.8 (95% CI 0.92–3.5, p=0.09) for the same outcome across 5 trials (I² = 67%). How should you interpret these discordant results?
opts: A. The individual trial is definitive; meta-analysis likely underpowered with high heterogeneity
B. The meta-analysis supersedes the single trial; the therapy likely has no significant effect
C. High heterogeneity (I²=67%) makes meta-analysis results unreliable; neither result is definitive; clinical context needed
D. Both results show benefit (OR >1); the difference in significance is purely due to sample size
exp: I² = 67% indicates substantial heterogeneity — the variation in results across studies is not due to chance. When I² is high (>50-75%), pooling results in a meta-analysis is questionable and the summary OR may be misleading. The discordance (single trial significant, meta-analysis not) could reflect: (1) heterogeneous patient populations across trials, (2) different drug doses or durations, or (3) true inconsistency. The correct interpretation is that neither result is definitive and the clinical context/sources of heterogeneity must be explored. Publication bias and subgroup analyses should also be considered.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Biostatistics; Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews

q: A pharmacoeconomic analysis of a new hepatitis C drug claims: ICER = $42,000/QALY (base case). The report states the result is 'robust' based on a deterministic sensitivity analysis varying costs ±25%. A reviewer argues this is insufficient. What additional analysis is needed?
opts: A. Budget impact analysis (BIA) — examines affordability at population level
B. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) — Monte Carlo simulation to quantify parameter uncertainty simultaneously across all variables
C. Threshold analysis — identifies at what price the drug crosses the willingness-to-pay threshold
D. Subgroup analysis stratified by genotype — heterogeneity in treatment effect affects ICER
exp: Deterministic (one-way or two-way) sensitivity analysis tests model robustness by varying one or two parameters at a time. It does NOT capture the joint uncertainty across all model parameters simultaneously. Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis (PSA) uses Monte Carlo simulation to sample from probability distributions for all input parameters simultaneously, generating a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC) and confidence intervals around the ICER. PSA is the gold standard for quantifying model uncertainty in CEAs. BIA is separate (affordability, not cost-effectiveness). Threshold analysis is useful but less comprehensive than PSA.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Pharmacoeconomics; ISPOR Guidelines for Economic Modeling

q: A pharmacist receives a complex drug information question about a novel oncology agent. The tertiary databases (Micromedex, Lexicomp) have no data. The package insert mentions one phase I dose-escalation study (n=12). What is the appropriate evidence hierarchy approach?
opts: A. Use the package insert data; it represents the most up-to-date manufacturer information
B. Search PubMed for primary literature, then conference abstracts; acknowledge quality limitations
C. Rely on the manufacturer's medical information line as the definitive answer; an independent literature search is unnecessary
D. Declare insufficient evidence and recommend standard of care without the new agent
exp: The systematic approach to drug information moves from tertiary sources to secondary sources, which are searched for primary literature. When tertiary references have no data, the next step is to search secondary databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase) for published trials. Then search conference proceedings (ASCO, ASH, ESMO) for newer unpublished data, and appraise and acknowledge the limits of small early-phase studies. The manufacturer's medical information department is a useful supplementary source (it may have unpublished data), but it is not independent and does not replace a literature search. A is wrong: the package insert reflects approval data and may lag newer literature. C is wrong: depending on the manufacturer alone gives up independent, critically appraised evidence. D is wrong: declaring insufficient evidence without searching the primary literature is premature.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Drug Information Resources; Malone et al. Drug Information Textbook

q: A hospital pharmacy is implementing a pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship program (ASP). The program wants to measure process and outcome metrics. Which metric pair BEST reflects both process and outcome?
opts: A. Days of therapy (DOT)/1000 patient-days AND C. difficile incidence per 10,000 patient-days
B. Number of interventions documented AND total cost savings
C. Percentage of restricted antibiotic approvals AND length of stay
D. Time to antibiotic therapy AND 30-day readmission rates
exp: IDSA/SHEA ASP guidelines recommend both PROCESS metrics (what the program does) and OUTCOME metrics (what happens to patients/institution): Process: Days of Therapy (DOT)/1,000 patient-days (standardizes antibiotic use independent of census) — directly measures ASP intervention impact. Outcome: C. difficile infection rate per 10,000 patient-days — a sentinel event reflecting selective antibiotic pressure on the gut microbiome. Together these measure stewardship activity AND its clinical impact. The pairing in option A is the standard endorsed by IDSA/SHEA.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; IDSA/SHEA Antimicrobial Stewardship Guidelines 2016

q: A pharmacy director is evaluating a formulary request for a biosimilar to adalimumab. The biosimilar has an FDA designation as 'interchangeable.' What does interchangeable designation mean, and what authority does the pharmacist have?
opts: A. Interchangeable means clinically equivalent; pharmacist may substitute without prescriber notification in all 50 states
B. Interchangeable designation means pharmacist CAN substitute without prescriber consent per FDA, but state law governs actual substitution authority — must check state pharmacy practice act
C. Interchangeable means the biosimilar was proven equivalent in a switching study; substitution requires prescriber approval in all cases
D. Interchangeable designation does not exist for monoclonal antibodies; all biologics require prescriber authorization
exp: Under the Public Health Service Act section 351(k)(4), an interchangeable biosimilar must be biosimilar to the reference product and be expected to produce the same clinical result in any given patient. For products given more than once, the risk of alternating or switching between the products must be no greater than continued use of the reference product. An interchangeable product may be substituted for the reference product without the intervention of the prescriber (section 351(i)(3)). Whether and how a pharmacist may actually substitute, including prescriber and patient notification and record-keeping, is set by each state's pharmacy practice law. B is correct. A is wrong: substitution rules and notification requirements vary by state. C is wrong: interchangeability allows substitution without prescriber approval, and switching studies are not required in every case. D is wrong: monoclonal antibodies can be designated interchangeable; several adalimumab biosimilars (e.g., Cyltezo, 2021) hold this designation. In June 2024 FDA issued draft guidance stating that switching studies generally are no longer expected to show interchangeability. The 2019 guidance had expected them.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; FDA Biosimilar Guidance; NABP Model Pharmacy Practice Act

q: A landmark trial is criticized because 28% of patients randomized to placebo crossed over to the active drug arm at week 8 due to disease progression. The primary endpoint (ITT analysis) showed HR=0.72 (p=0.04) favoring the drug. A per-protocol analysis shows HR=0.61 (p=0.001). How does crossover affect interpretation?
opts: A. ITT analysis underestimates the true treatment effect because crossover dilutes the comparison
B. Per-protocol analysis should be used as primary since it captures actual drug exposure
C. Both analyses are biased; only rank-preserved structural nested models can correct for crossover
D. Crossover only affects safety analysis; efficacy is unaffected in randomized trials
exp: High crossover from control to active arm biases ITT analysis TOWARD THE NULL (underestimates true treatment effect) because control patients eventually receive the active drug, making outcomes in both arms more similar. This is why the ITT HR (0.72) is less pronounced than per-protocol (0.61). However, per-protocol analysis introduces selection bias (patients remaining on treatment may differ systematically). Statistical approaches like rank-preserved structural failure time models (RPSFTM) or two-stage adjustment can better estimate the true treatment effect. The ITT remains the primary analysis but must be interpreted in context of crossover.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2, Study Design; CONSORT; Crossover adjustment statistical methods

q: A non-inferiority trial compared oral sotalol with IV amiodarone for AF cardioversion using a non-inferiority margin of 10 percentage points. Cardioversion success was 66% with amiodarone and 62% with sotalol (absolute difference −4%; 95% CI for the difference −10% to +2%). What conclusion is correct?
opts: A. Sotalol is non-inferior — the CI upper bound (+2%) is within the margin
B. Sotalol is non-inferior — the lower bound (-10%) does not exceed the -10% non-inferiority margin
C. Results are inconclusive — the confidence interval just touches the non-inferiority margin at -10%, which does not establish non-inferiority
D. Sotalol is inferior — the point estimate shows lower success rate (62% vs 66%)
exp: Difference = 62% − 66% = −4%. The 95% CI (−10% to +2%) is centered on the point estimate: (−10 + 2)/2 = −4. Non-inferiority is shown only when the whole CI lies above −Δ, meaning the lower bound is strictly greater than −10%. Here the lower bound equals −10%, so a 10-point loss of efficacy cannot be ruled out and non-inferiority is not established. The upper bound (+2%) crosses zero, so sotalol is also not shown to be inferior. The result is inconclusive. A is wrong: the upper bound has no bearing on non-inferiority. B is wrong: a lower bound equal to the margin does not exclude it (FDA 2016 NI guidance; CONSORT NI extension). D is wrong: a lower point estimate with a CI that includes 0 does not show inferiority.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; CONSORT NI Trial Reporting; FDA NI Guidance 2016

q: A drug has a Ki of 2 nM at CYP3A4. At steady-state plasma concentrations of 50 nM, what is the expected fold-increase in exposure ([I]/Ki + 1) for a substrate where this is the sole clearance pathway?
opts: A. 24-fold increase in AUC for the substrate
B. 26-fold increase in AUC for the substrate
C. 52-fold increase in AUC for the substrate
D. 50-fold increase in AUC for the substrate
exp: Using the reversible inhibition equation: AUC ratio = 1 / (1 - (I/(I+Ki))) or for competitive inhibition AUC ratio = 1 + I/Ki (simplified for inhibitor effect on clearance via the Rowland-Matin equation when fm=1). If [I]/Ki = 50/2 = 25, then the inhibition quotient = 25+1 = 26 (the substrate's AUC is expected to increase approximately 26-fold). This is the [I]/Ki + 1 approach used in FDA drug interaction guidance. FDA considers [I]/Ki ≥ 0.1 a positive signal for in vitro DDI studies, and ≥ 25 signals a very potent inhibitor.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 2; FDA Drug Interaction Guidance; Rowland-Matin equation

q: A 26-year-old woman is prescribed doxycycline 100mg BID for 7 days for Chlamydia infection. She is also on combined oral contraceptives (OCP). She asks whether the antibiotic affects OCP efficacy. What is the evidence-based counseling?
opts: A. Yes, doxycycline significantly reduces OCP efficacy via gut flora disruption; use backup contraception during and 7 days after
B. No significant pharmacokinetic interaction — doxycycline does not affect CYP3A4 or gut-flora mediated OCP enterohepatic cycling in studies; backup contraception not required
C. Doxycycline is a CYP3A4 inducer; reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by 40%; requires backup method
D. Only rifampin and anticonvulsants affect OCP; all other antibiotics are safe
exp: Current evidence (multiple PK studies) does NOT support a clinically meaningful reduction in OCP efficacy with most antibiotics (including doxycycline, amoxicillin, ampicillin). The theoretical gut-flora disruption hypothesis has not been confirmed in clinical studies. ACOG, WHO, CDC, and major contraception guidelines updated their guidance: routine backup contraception is NOT required with non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics. The exceptions that DO require backup: enzyme-inducing drugs (rifampin/rifabutin, certain anticonvulsants like phenytoin/carbamazepine).
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; ACOG Practice Bulletin; CDC Medical Eligibility Criteria

q: A stable adult kidney transplant recipient has non-severe CMV disease, adequate oral absorption, and Cockcroft–Gault CrCl 38 mL/min. Which oral valganciclovir treatment dose follows adult renal dosing?
opts: A. 900 mg twice daily
B. 450 mg once daily
C. 450 mg every two days
D. 900 mg once daily
exp: At CrCl 25–39 mL/min, the adult treatment dose is 450 mg once daily. Monitor renal function, CBC, virologic response, and the need for IV treatment if severity or absorption changes.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; AST/IDSA CMV Guidelines; Transplant ID
opts_exp: A. 900 mg twice daily is the usual adult treatment dose at CrCl ≥60 mL/min.
B. Correct. At CrCl 25–39 mL/min, the adult treatment dose is 450 mg once daily. Monitor renal function, CBC, virologic response, and the need for IV treatment if severity or absorption changes.
C. 450 mg every two days is the prevention dose at CrCl 25–39, not the treatment dose.
D. 900 mg daily is not the labeled treatment dose for CrCl 38.
reviewNote: Targeted correction 2026-10-19; full chapter review pending.

q: A 68-year-old woman is on heparin infusion post-mechanical valve replacement. On day 7, platelet count drops from 220,000 to 54,000. 4T score is calculated: Thrombocytopenia >50% (2), timing day 5-10 (2), thrombosis none (0), other cause unlikely (1) = 5/8. What is the appropriate management?
opts: A. Stop heparin, begin direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban or bivalirudin); check HIT antibody (SRA or PF4-ELISA)
B. Continue heparin; thrombocytopenia is expected post-cardiac surgery (HIT-1)
C. Reduce heparin dose by 50% and recheck platelet count in 24 hours
D. Transfuse platelets to maintain >50,000 and continue heparin for valve protection
exp: 4T score 5-8 = HIGH probability of HIT. Management: STOP all heparin products IMMEDIATELY (including heparin flushes, LMWH). Start alternative anticoagulation with a non-heparin agent: argatroban (preferred with normal liver function) or bivalirudin. Send HIT antibody testing (PF4/heparin IgG ELISA for screening; serotonin release assay for confirmation). Do NOT transfuse platelets (may worsen thrombosis). Warfarin should not be started until platelets recover to >150,000 (risk of venous limb gangrene).
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; ACCP HIT Management Guidelines

q: A 74-year-old man is admitted to ICU with cardiogenic shock (SBP 78 mmHg, CI 1.6 L/min/m², pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 26 mmHg, SVR 2200 dyn·sec/cm⁵) after anterior STEMI. He is on dopamine 10 mcg/kg/min. Which vasopressor/inotrope change is supported by evidence?
opts: A. Add vasopressin 0.03 units/min to reduce dopamine dose
B. Switch dopamine to norepinephrine + dobutamine — SOAP-II trial: dopamine increases arrhythmia and mortality in CS
C. Increase dopamine to 20 mcg/kg/min — dose-dependent cardiac output improvement
D. Add milrinone 0.375-0.75 mcg/kg/min — PDE3 inhibitor increases CI without vasoconstriction
exp: SOAP-II trial: Dopamine vs. norepinephrine for shock — in the cardiogenic shock subgroup, dopamine was associated with higher 28-day mortality and significantly more arrhythmias. Current guidelines recommend norepinephrine as the vasopressor of choice for cardiogenic shock with hypotension. Adding dobutamine (2.5-20 mcg/kg/min) addresses the low CI (inotropy) while norepinephrine maintains perfusion pressure. Milrinone is an alternative inotrope but causes more hypotension (vasodilation) and is problematic in severe hypotension.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; SOAP-II Trial; AHA Cardiogenic Shock Scientific Statement 2019

q: A 45-year-old alcoholic patient with liver cirrhosis presents with serum sodium 112 mEq/L. He is asymptomatic (no seizures, no altered mental status). Rate of sodium correction for asymptomatic severe hyponatremia is:
opts: A. Correct at 1-2 mEq/L/hr until sodium is 130 mEq/L — prevent cerebral edema
B. Correct no more than 8 mEq/L in the first 24h, 18 mEq/L in 48h — prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS)
C. Correct no more than 10-12 mEq/L in 24h or 18 mEq/L in 48h; for high-risk patients (alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease) limit to 8 mEq/L/24h
D. Aggressive correction to 125 mEq/L within 4-6 hours is safe for asymptomatic hyponatremia
exp: Correction limits for hyponatremia: Typically no more than 10-12 mEq/L in 24h or 18 mEq/L in 48h to prevent ODS (osmotic demyelination syndrome / central pontine myelinolysis). For HIGH-RISK patients (alcoholism, malnutrition, advanced liver disease, hypokalemia, prior hypoxia) the limit is stricter: ≤8 mEq/L in 24h. This patient is an alcoholic with liver cirrhosis = high risk → 8 mEq/L/24h maximum. Overly rapid correction causes ODS, an irreversible demyelinating injury. If overcorrection occurs, D5W ± desmopressin can re-lower sodium.
ref: ACCP 2024 Vol 1; SIADH/Hyponatremia Clinical Practice Guidelines

q: An IV drug follows linear kinetics. Clearance is 5 L/hour and the desired average steady-state concentration is 8 mg/L. What maintenance infusion rate produces that average concentration?
opts: A. 1.6 mg/hour
B. 13 mg/hour
C. 40 mg/hour
D. 625 mg/hour
exp: Rate = clearance × target concentration = 5 × 8 = 40 mg/hour.
opts_exp: A. Dividing concentration by clearance gives the wrong units.
B. Adding clearance and concentration is not dimensionally valid.
C. Correct. Rate = clearance × target concentration = 5 × 8 = 40 mg/hour.
D. Squaring clearance is not part of the maintenance-rate equation.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 3: Pharmacokinetics

q: A hypothetical drug has a volume of distribution of 30 L. For an IV bolus target of 6 mg/L, what loading dose is predicted before accounting for practical formulation limits?
opts: A. 36 mg
B. 180 mg
C. 360 mg
D. 5 mg
exp: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration / F; IV F = 1, so 30 × 6 = 180 mg.
opts_exp: A. This does not equal volume × concentration.
B. Correct. Loading dose = Vd × target concentration / F; IV F = 1, so 30 × 6 = 180 mg.
C. This doubles the calculated loading dose without justification.
D. Concentration must be multiplied by volume, not divided.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 3: Pharmacokinetics

q: A drug has first-order elimination and a 6-hour half-life. With no further doses, what fraction remains 18 hours after a dose?
exp: 18 hours is three half-lives: (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 12.5%.
opts_exp: A. Correct. 18 hours is three half-lives: (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 12.5%.
B. 6.25% remains after four half-lives (24 hours).
C. 50% remains after one half-life (6 hours).
D. 25% remains after two half-lives (12 hours).
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 3: Pharmacokinetics

q: In a randomized trial, a harmful event occurs in 18% of controls and 12% of treated participants over one year. What is the absolute risk reduction?
opts: A. 150 percentage points
B. 6 percentage points
C. 33 percentage points
D. 50 percentage points
exp: ARR = control risk − treatment risk = 18% − 12% = 6 percentage points.
opts_exp: A. An absolute reduction cannot exceed 100 percentage points.
B. Correct. ARR = control risk − treatment risk = 18% − 12% = 6 percentage points.
C. 33% is approximately the relative risk reduction, not the absolute reduction.
D. This is not the difference between the two risks.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 10: Biostatistics

q: A one-year trial reports risks of 20% with control and 15% with treatment. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one event over that year?
exp: NNT = 1/(0.20 − 0.15) = 20 for the stated one-year follow-up.
opts_exp: A. Five is the absolute risk reduction in percentage points, not NNT.
B. Correct. NNT = 1/(0.20 − 0.15) = 20 for the stated one-year follow-up.
C. 25% is the relative risk reduction, not NNT.
D. Using 1% rather than the actual 5% ARR yields this error.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 10: Biostatistics

q: A superiority trial estimates a risk ratio of 0.82 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.66–1.03. Which interpretation is best?
opts: A. The null value is excluded
B. The result does not establish superiority at the conventional two-sided 0.05 level
C. There is an 82% chance that the treatment works
D. The treatment has proved equivalent
exp: The confidence interval includes 1, so this analysis does not establish superiority at the corresponding conventional significance level.
opts_exp: A. The null ratio of 1 is inside this confidence interval.
B. Correct. The confidence interval includes 1, so this analysis does not establish superiority at the corresponding conventional significance level.
C. A risk ratio is an effect estimate, not a probability that the treatment works.
D. Failure to show superiority does not establish equivalence.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 10: Biostatistics

q: Investigators randomly assign participants to two treatments, then analyze them in their assigned groups despite some crossovers. Which analysis principle is this?
opts: A. Case-control sampling
B. Historical control analysis
C. Per-protocol
D. Intention-to-treat
exp: Intention-to-treat retains participants in their randomized groups, helping preserve randomization.
opts_exp: A. Case-control sampling starts with outcome status rather than randomized assignment.
B. Both groups here are concurrent randomized groups.
C. Per-protocol generally restricts analysis to participants meeting protocol criteria.
D. Correct. Intention-to-treat retains participants in their randomized groups, helping preserve randomization.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 11: Study Designs

q: A study identifies people with a rare adverse event and a comparison group without it, then examines prior drug exposure. Which design is described?
opts: A. Single-patient case report
B. Prospective randomized trial
C. Case-control study
D. Cross-sectional prevalence survey
exp: A case-control study selects by outcome status and compares earlier exposures.
opts_exp: A. The design contains cases and a comparison group, not one descriptive case.
B. Treatment was not assigned randomly.
C. Correct. A case-control study selects by outcome status and compares earlier exposures.
D. The study looks backward at exposure rather than measuring a single-time prevalence sample.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 11: Study Designs

q: A randomized trial cannot blind participants, but the committee classifying outcomes does not know treatment assignments. Which bias is this committee blinding most directly intended to reduce?
opts: A. Outcome assessment bias
B. Random sampling error
C. Loss to follow-up
D. Publication bias
exp: Blinded adjudication reduces the chance that knowledge of treatment changes outcome classification.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Blinded adjudication reduces the chance that knowledge of treatment changes outcome classification.
B. Blinding does not eliminate random error from finite sample size.
C. Blinded adjudication does not itself prevent missing follow-up.
D. Publication bias concerns which studies become available, not within-study adjudication.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 11: Study Designs

q: Before dispensing prasugrel after PCI, a pharmacist discovers a documented prior transient ischemic attack. What is the most appropriate response?
opts: A. Hold verification and contact the team about the contraindication
B. Reduce prasugrel to every other day
C. Add aspirin to remove the contraindication
D. Dispense unchanged because the TIA was transient
exp: Prasugrel is contraindicated with a history of stroke or TIA; the team should select an appropriate alternative.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Prasugrel is contraindicated with a history of stroke or TIA; the team should select an appropriate alternative.
B. An unvalidated alternate-day schedule does not resolve the contraindication.
C. Aspirin does not negate the intracranial bleeding concern.
D. A prior TIA is relevant even if symptoms resolved.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 1: Acute Care Cardiology

q: Which finding most directly distinguishes STEMI from an isolated laboratory diagnosis of myocardial injury?
opts: A. A compatible acute ischemic presentation with diagnostic ST-segment elevation
B. A history of hypertension alone
C. A positive troponin alone
D. A coronary calcium score alone
exp: STEMI is an acute ischemic syndrome with diagnostic ECG changes; reperfusion evaluation should not wait for a positive troponin.
opts_exp: A. Correct. STEMI is an acute ischemic syndrome with diagnostic ECG changes; reperfusion evaluation should not wait for a positive troponin.
B. Hypertension is a risk factor rather than a diagnostic finding.
C. Troponin elevation can occur with many non-STEMI and nonischemic conditions.
D. Coronary calcium does not diagnose an acute STEMI.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 1: Acute Care Cardiology

q: A patient took sildenafil earlier today and now has ischemic chest discomfort. Which order warrants an immediate interaction check before administration?
opts: A. Clopidogrel
B. Aspirin
C. Nitroglycerin
D. Atorvastatin
exp: Nitrates with recent sildenafil can cause profound hypotension; clarify timing and use an appropriate alternative plan.
opts_exp: A. Clopidogrel is not a nitrate and does not share this interaction mechanism.
B. Aspirin does not have the nitrate–PDE5 interaction.
C. Correct. Nitrates with recent sildenafil can cause profound hypotension; clarify timing and use an appropriate alternative plan.
D. Atorvastatin is not the acute hypotensive interaction described.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 1: Acute Care Cardiology

q: Which beta-blocker has evidence supporting survival benefit in chronic HFrEF?
opts: A. Metoprolol succinate extended release
B. Propranolol as-needed
C. Atenolol solely for convenience
D. Metoprolol tartrate is interchangeable with succinate for the trial evidence
exp: Metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, and bisoprolol are the evidence-based HFrEF beta-blockers.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, and bisoprolol are the evidence-based HFrEF beta-blockers.
B. As-needed propranolol is not an evidence-based HFrEF regimen.
C. Atenolol is not one of the three beta-blockers supported by the major HFrEF survival trials.
D. The formulation used in the HFrEF evidence matters; tartrate is not an equivalent evidence substitute.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 2: Chronic Care Cardiology

q: A patient takes lisinopril and is to start sacubitril/valsartan. Which transition requirement is correct?
opts: A. Separate the last ACE inhibitor dose and first ARNI dose by at least 36 hours
B. Use a 36-hour washout only for an ARB
C. Double the lisinopril dose during the transition
D. Give both indefinitely
exp: A washout of at least 36 hours is required between an ACE inhibitor and sacubitril/valsartan.
opts_exp: A. Correct. A washout of at least 36 hours is required between an ACE inhibitor and sacubitril/valsartan.
B. The 36-hour requirement applies to ACE inhibitors, not a routine switch from an ARB.
C. Increasing ACE inhibition adds risk and does not facilitate transition.
D. Concurrent ACE inhibitor and ARNI use increases angioedema risk.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 2: Chronic Care Cardiology

q: Which regimen is classified as high-intensity statin therapy?
opts: A. Atorvastatin 80 mg daily
B. Rosuvastatin 5 mg daily
C. Pravastatin 10 mg daily
D. Simvastatin 10 mg daily
exp: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg is high intensity, expected to lower LDL-C by at least 50% on average.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Atorvastatin 40–80 mg is high intensity, expected to lower LDL-C by at least 50% on average.
B. Rosuvastatin 5 mg is moderate intensity.
C. Pravastatin 10 mg is low intensity.
D. Simvastatin 10 mg is low intensity.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 2: Chronic Care Cardiology

q: A patient with a mechanical mitral valve asks to replace warfarin with apixaban to avoid INR testing. Which response is best?
opts: A. Alternate warfarin and apixaban on successive days
B. Switch because all oral anticoagulants are equivalent
C. Continue a vitamin K antagonist plan; a DOAC is not an appropriate substitute for this valve
D. Use aspirin alone instead
exp: A mechanical mitral valve requires vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation with an individualized INR plan; apixaban is not a substitute.
opts_exp: A. Alternating agents is unvalidated and creates unsafe anticoagulation transitions.
B. Evidence and recommendations differ by indication; mechanical valves require a vitamin K antagonist.
C. Correct. A mechanical mitral valve requires vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation with an individualized INR plan; apixaban is not a substitute.
D. Antiplatelet monotherapy is inadequate for mechanical-valve anticoagulation.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 3: Anticoagulation

q: For nonvalvular AF, a patient is 83 years old, weighs 57 kg, and has serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. Assuming no other dosing modifiers, what apixaban dose follows the labeled age/weight/creatinine reduction rule?
opts: A. 5 mg twice daily
B. 2.5 mg twice daily
C. 5 mg once daily
D. No anticoagulation solely because of age
exp: The AF reduction rule is 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two criteria are met: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL.
opts_exp: A. Two reduction criteria are met: age at least 80 and weight at most 60 kg.
B. Correct. The AF reduction rule is 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two criteria are met: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL.
C. Once-daily dosing is not the labeled apixaban AF regimen.
D. Age alone does not establish a reason to withhold indicated stroke prevention.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 3: Anticoagulation

q: A patient receiving heparin develops a new thrombosis and a platelet fall consistent with a high clinical probability of HIT. What is the appropriate immediate medication approach while confirmatory testing is arranged?
opts: A. Stop all heparin and initiate an appropriate non-heparin anticoagulant if no contraindication
B. Switch from UFH to enoxaparin
C. Begin warfarin alone immediately
D. Continue heparin until testing returns
exp: High-probability HIT requires stopping heparin products and therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulation, adjusted for bleeding risk and clinical circumstances.
opts_exp: A. Correct. High-probability HIT requires stopping heparin products and therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulation, adjusted for bleeding risk and clinical circumstances.
B. LMWH can cross-react with HIT antibodies and is not an appropriate substitute.
C. Early warfarin monotherapy before platelet recovery can worsen thrombosis.
D. Waiting on heparin exposes a high-probability patient to further thrombosis.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 3: Anticoagulation

q: A patient has an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection without fever or flank pain. Why would nitrofurantoin become inappropriate if pyelonephritis were instead suspected?
opts: A. It treats only viruses
B. It is always bacteriostatic and therefore unusable
C. It never reaches urine
D. It lacks reliable renal tissue concentrations for upper-tract infection
exp: Nitrofurantoin is a lower-tract agent and does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal concentrations for pyelonephritis.
opts_exp: A. Nitrofurantoin is antibacterial.
B. Suitability depends on exposure at the infection site, not a blanket static/cidal rule.
C. Nitrofurantoin does concentrate in urine.
D. Correct. Nitrofurantoin is a lower-tract agent and does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal concentrations for pyelonephritis.
