ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 4: Infectious Diseases I

q: A patient with documented immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin needs an antibiotic. What information is most useful before assuming all beta-lactams are prohibited?
opts: A. The wholesale cost of penicillin
B. Only the color of the prior tablet
C. The culprit drug, reaction phenotype and timing, and side-chain relationships of proposed alternatives
D. Whether the patient prefers capsules
exp: A careful allergy history and structural cross-reactivity assessment can guide safe alternatives or formal allergy evaluation.
opts_exp: A. Cost does not determine anaphylaxis risk.
B. Tablet color does not characterize allergy risk.
C. Correct. A careful allergy history and structural cross-reactivity assessment can guide safe alternatives or formal allergy evaluation.
D. Formulation preference does not establish immunologic cross-reactivity.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 4: Infectious Diseases I

q: Which prescribing action most directly supports antimicrobial stewardship after blood cultures identify a susceptible pathogen?
opts: A. Continue all empiric agents indefinitely
B. Reassess source, susceptibilities, dose, and duration and narrow therapy when appropriate
C. Add a second agent for every positive culture
D. Ignore cultures once symptoms improve
exp: Culture-directed reassessment can reduce unnecessary spectrum while maintaining effective treatment at the infection site.
opts_exp: A. Indefinite broad therapy adds avoidable toxicity and selection pressure.
B. Correct. Culture-directed reassessment can reduce unnecessary spectrum while maintaining effective treatment at the infection site.
C. Combination therapy is not automatically indicated for every organism or syndrome.
D. Microbiologic findings should inform reassessment alongside the clinical response.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 4: Infectious Diseases I

q: A patient on a ritonavir-containing regimen starts a new prescription. Which process is essential?
opts: A. Check for clinically important metabolic and transporter interactions
B. Stop all chronic medications automatically
C. Space every medication by one hour to prevent all interactions
D. Assume the booster affects only antiretrovirals
exp: Ritonavir strongly affects CYP3A and other pathways; use a validated interaction resource and patient-specific plan.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Ritonavir strongly affects CYP3A and other pathways; use a validated interaction resource and patient-specific plan.
B. Automatic discontinuation without evaluating indication and interaction is unsafe.
C. Separating administration times does not eliminate enzyme-mediated interactions.
D. Ritonavir affects many non-antiretroviral medications.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 5: Infectious Diseases II

q: Why does daptomycin generally not serve as treatment for alveolar pneumonia?
opts: A. It has no activity against gram-positive organisms
B. It must always be administered orally
C. It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant
D. It is not an antibacterial drug
exp: Pulmonary surfactant inactivates daptomycin, limiting use for alveolar pneumonia.
opts_exp: A. Its clinical spectrum includes important gram-positive pathogens.
B. Daptomycin is administered intravenously.
C. Correct. Pulmonary surfactant inactivates daptomycin, limiting use for alveolar pneumonia.
D. Daptomycin is an antibacterial lipopeptide.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 5: Infectious Diseases II

q: A patient taking an echinocandin for candidemia asks why the team is checking blood cultures again. Which answer is best?
opts: A. To determine a vancomycin trough
B. To document bloodstream clearance and guide treatment duration
C. Because a single positive culture always represents contamination
D. Because susceptibility testing replaces the need for clearance
exp: Repeat blood cultures help establish clearance; treatment duration also depends on clinical response and complications.
opts_exp: A. Vancomycin monitoring is unrelated to fungal bloodstream clearance.
B. Correct. Repeat blood cultures help establish clearance; treatment duration also depends on clinical response and complications.
C. Candida in blood should be taken seriously.
D. Susceptibility and bloodstream clearance answer different questions.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 5: Infectious Diseases II

q: A patient in septic shock remains hypotensive despite appropriate initial fluid assessment and resuscitation. Which vasopressor is generally first line?
opts: A. Norepinephrine
B. Phenylephrine for every patient
C. Dopamine for every patient
D. Oral midodrine instead of IV support
exp: Norepinephrine is the usual first-line vasopressor in septic shock, with titration and ongoing perfusion assessment.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Norepinephrine is the usual first-line vasopressor in septic shock, with titration and ongoing perfusion assessment.
B. Phenylephrine is not the routine first-line agent for all septic shock.
C. Dopamine has greater arrhythmia risk and is not the default.
D. Oral midodrine does not replace urgent IV support for unstable shock.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 6: Critical Care

q: During a continuous neuromuscular blocker infusion, which principle is essential?
opts: A. Provide and assess adequate analgesia and sedation independently of paralysis
B. Stop sedation because movement is absent
C. Use a train-of-four response to measure pain
D. Paralysis proves the patient is comfortable
exp: Analgesia and sedation must be ensured; paralysis can conceal distress and awareness.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Analgesia and sedation must be ensured; paralysis can conceal distress and awareness.
B. Absent movement is not evidence of adequate sedation.
C. Train-of-four assesses neuromuscular blockade, not pain or awareness.
D. Neuromuscular blockade does not provide analgesia or amnesia.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 6: Critical Care

q: A hypotensive ventilated patient is receiving propofol. Which observation should trigger reassessment of the sedation plan?
opts: A. An appropriately documented pain assessment
B. An intact medication label
C. A fall in blood pressure temporally associated with dose escalation
D. A stable sedation target
exp: Propofol can cause dose-related hypotension; reassess dose, hemodynamics, and alternative causes promptly.
opts_exp: A. Pain assessment is appropriate rather than a reason by itself to change sedation.
B. Correct labeling is necessary but does not signal physiologic intolerance.
C. Correct. Propofol can cause dose-related hypotension; reassess dose, hemodynamics, and alternative causes promptly.
D. Meeting the sedation target alone does not identify a drug complication.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 6: Critical Care

q: A serum potassium result is markedly elevated, but the specimen is reported as hemolyzed and the patient has no ECG changes. What is the best next step?
opts: A. Diagnose chronic hypokalemia
B. Ignore the result permanently
C. Promptly assess the patient and repeat an appropriate specimen while evaluating urgency
D. Administer potassium replacement
exp: Assess for clinical/ECG danger and promptly confirm a potentially spurious result; do not delay emergency treatment if instability is present.
opts_exp: A. The reported result does not establish hypokalemia.
B. A hemolyzed specimen can be misleading, but dangerous true hyperkalemia must still be considered.
C. Correct. Assess for clinical/ECG danger and promptly confirm a potentially spurious result; do not delay emergency treatment if instability is present.
D. Potassium replacement could worsen true hyperkalemia.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 7: Fluids, Electrolytes & Nutrition

q: A severely malnourished patient starts nutrition and develops a rapid fall in phosphate. Which complication should be considered?
opts: A. Refeeding syndrome
B. Acute aspirin allergy
C. Isolated iron overload
D. Vitamin K excess
exp: Refeeding can shift phosphate, potassium, and magnesium intracellularly; identify risk, give thiamine as appropriate, and monitor/replace electrolytes.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Refeeding can shift phosphate, potassium, and magnesium intracellularly; identify risk, give thiamine as appropriate, and monitor/replace electrolytes.
B. This electrolyte pattern is not characteristic of aspirin allergy.
C. Iron overload does not explain the timing with restarting nutrition.
D. Vitamin K excess does not account for the characteristic phosphate shift.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 7: Fluids, Electrolytes & Nutrition

q: An IV bag contains 40 mEq of potassium in 1000 mL. How many mEq are delivered in 250 mL?
opts: A. 10 mEq
B. 20 mEq
C. 160 mEq
D. 5 mEq
exp: 40 mEq × 250/1000 = 10 mEq; administration rate and route require separate safety checks.
opts_exp: A. Correct. 40 mEq × 250/1000 = 10 mEq; administration rate and route require separate safety checks.
B. 20 mEq would be delivered in half the bag.
C. This reverses the volume ratio.
D. 250 mL is one quarter, not one eighth, of the bag.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 7: Fluids, Electrolytes & Nutrition

q: A patient taking lithium develops vomiting, poor intake, and a new NSAID prescription. What medication concern deserves prompt assessment?
opts: A. A guaranteed need to double lithium
B. Prevention of lithium toxicity by dehydration
C. Lithium accumulation and toxicity
D. Loss of all lithium absorption
exp: Volume depletion and NSAIDs can reduce lithium clearance; assess symptoms, renal function, level, and medication plan promptly.
opts_exp: A. Empiric doubling could worsen toxicity.
B. Dehydration can increase, not prevent, toxicity risk.
C. Correct. Volume depletion and NSAIDs can reduce lithium clearance; assess symptoms, renal function, level, and medication plan promptly.
D. These factors do not reliably eliminate absorption.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 8: Psychiatry

q: Which counseling point is correct for bupropion?
opts: A. It is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
B. It has no effect on seizure risk
C. A seizure disorder is a contraindication
D. It is always preferred in active bulimia nervosa
exp: A seizure disorder is a labeled contraindication to bupropion.
opts_exp: A. Bupropion is not an MAOI.
B. Bupropion has dose-related seizure risk.
C. Correct. A seizure disorder is a labeled contraindication to bupropion.
D. Current or prior bulimia/anorexia nervosa is also a contraindication because of seizure risk.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 8: Psychiatry

q: Which distinction remains important when studying older clozapine REMS material?
opts: A. Removal of REMS means neutropenia no longer occurs
B. Program requirements and clinical ANC monitoring are separate issues
C. Clozapine has no hematologic warning
D. ANC is a measure of renal clearance
exp: The US REMS was removed in 2025, while severe neutropenia risk and label-directed ANC monitoring remain relevant.
opts_exp: A. Removing an administrative program does not remove the biologic risk.
B. Correct. The US REMS was removed in 2025, while severe neutropenia risk and label-directed ANC monitoring remain relevant.
C. Severe neutropenia remains a serious clozapine risk.
D. ANC is the absolute neutrophil count, not a renal measurement.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 8: Psychiatry

q: A patient taking an enzyme-inducing antiseizure drug asks about a new oral contraceptive. What should the pharmacist evaluate?
opts: A. A guaranteed increase in contraceptive effectiveness
B. Only the tablet size
C. Whether spacing doses by five minutes eliminates the interaction
D. Possible reduction in contraceptive exposure and effectiveness
exp: Enzyme induction can reduce exposure to some hormonal contraceptives; assess the specific method and discuss reliable alternatives.
opts_exp: A. Enzyme induction generally lowers exposure to susceptible substrates.
B. Tablet size does not characterize the interaction.
C. Dose spacing does not remove sustained enzyme induction.
D. Correct. Enzyme induction can reduce exposure to some hormonal contraceptives; assess the specific method and discuss reliable alternatives.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 9: Neurology

q: A patient has low albumin and a total phenytoin concentration that appears subtherapeutic but has nystagmus and ataxia. Which assessment is best?
opts: A. Assume the symptoms exclude phenytoin toxicity
B. Use serum sodium as a direct phenytoin level
C. Increase the dose solely to normalize the total level
D. Consider an elevated free fraction and obtain a free concentration when available
exp: Free phenytoin and the clinical picture are especially useful when protein binding is altered.
opts_exp: A. Nystagmus and ataxia can be manifestations of phenytoin toxicity.
B. Sodium is not a phenytoin concentration assay.
C. A low total level can conceal excessive unbound exposure in hypoalbuminemia.
D. Correct. Free phenytoin and the clinical picture are especially useful when protein binding is altered.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 9: Neurology

q: A patient takes levodopa/carbidopa and asks why carbidopa is included. Which explanation is correct?
opts: A. It is a replacement for levodopa
B. It inhibits peripheral levodopa decarboxylation
C. It blocks all brain dopamine receptors
D. It eliminates Parkinson disease progression
exp: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase, increasing levodopa available for the CNS and reducing peripheral adverse effects.
opts_exp: A. Carbidopa supports levodopa; it does not replace its central dopamine precursor role.
B. Correct. Carbidopa inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase, increasing levodopa available for the CNS and reducing peripheral adverse effects.
C. Dopamine receptor blockade would oppose the intended therapy.
D. The combination treats symptoms rather than eliminating progression.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 9: Neurology

q: A patient taking a combined estrogen-containing contraceptive reports migraine with aura. What is the appropriate medication review concern?
opts: A. Estrogen-associated stroke risk makes this method inappropriate
B. Aura guarantees protection against stroke
C. Adding more estrogen removes the concern
D. Only the brand name matters
exp: Migraine with aura is a contraindication to combined hormonal contraception; discuss an appropriate alternative.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Migraine with aura is a contraindication to combined hormonal contraception; discuss an appropriate alternative.
B. Aura is associated with increased stroke risk.
C. Increasing estrogen does not remove vascular risk.
D. The estrogen-containing method and risk factors matter, not simply brand.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 10: Sexual & Reproductive Health

q: For symptomatic Graves disease requiring an antithyroid drug during the first trimester, which option is generally preferred?
opts: A. Propylthiouracil
B. No treatment regardless of severity
C. Methimazole is always risk free
D. Radioactive iodine
exp: PTU is generally preferred in the first trimester because methimazole-associated embryopathy is a concern; both drugs require individualized risk assessment and monitoring.
opts_exp: A. Correct. PTU is generally preferred in the first trimester because methimazole-associated embryopathy is a concern; both drugs require individualized risk assessment and monitoring.
B. Untreated significant hyperthyroidism can harm the pregnant patient and fetus.
C. Methimazole is not risk free in the first trimester.
D. Radioactive iodine is contraindicated during pregnancy.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 10: Sexual & Reproductive Health

q: A patient asks whether condoms are still useful when a highly effective contraceptive method is used. Which response is best?
opts: A. An IUD prevents every STI
B. Hormonal contraception replaces all barrier protection
C. No method can reduce STI transmission
D. Condoms can add protection against sexually transmitted infections
exp: Condoms can provide STI protection beyond the pregnancy prevention of another method.
opts_exp: A. An IUD does not provide STI protection.
B. Hormonal contraception does not replace STI prevention measures.
C. Correct condom use reduces transmission risk for many STIs.
D. Correct. Condoms can provide STI protection beyond the pregnancy prevention of another method.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 10: Sexual & Reproductive Health

q: A pharmacist identifies a near miss before a wrong drug reaches the patient. Which response best supports a learning system?
opts: A. Wait until the same error causes injury
B. Suppress it because no harm occurred
C. Report and analyze the process vulnerability through the safety system
D. Blame the last person without investigation
exp: Reporting near misses can identify system weaknesses and guide prevention without waiting for harm.
opts_exp: A. Waiting forfeits a chance to prevent harm.
B. Near misses reveal vulnerabilities before injury occurs.
C. Correct. Reporting near misses can identify system weaknesses and guide prevention without waiting for harm.
D. Individual blame alone can obscure system contributors.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 1: Healthcare Systems

q: At discharge, two medication lists disagree about whether an ACE inhibitor was stopped for angioedema. Which action is best?
opts: A. Choose the longer list automatically
B. Resolve the discrepancy with the treating team before finalizing instructions
C. Tell the patient to take both lists
D. Delete the allergy record to make the lists match
exp: Medication reconciliation requires resolving discrepancies, documenting the reason, and communicating an accurate plan.
opts_exp: A. List length does not establish accuracy or safety.
B. Correct. Medication reconciliation requires resolving discrepancies, documenting the reason, and communicating an accurate plan.
C. Contradictory instructions increase medication harm.
D. Removing a relevant allergy to hide a discrepancy is unsafe.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 1: Healthcare Systems

q: An order says insulin 10 U, and the handwritten U could be read as a zero. Which prevention approach best addresses this risk?
opts: A. Use U more often so staff learn it
B. Allow concentration to remain unspecified
C. Rely on memory rather than verification
D. Write out units and use standardized electronic ordering
exp: Writing units in full and using standardized ordering reduces this avoidable abbreviation hazard.
opts_exp: A. Repeating an error-prone abbreviation does not remove ambiguity.
B. Unspecified insulin concentration adds a separate dosing risk.
C. Memory does not replace clear communication and verification.
D. Correct. Writing units in full and using standardized ordering reduces this avoidable abbreviation hazard.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 1: Healthcare Systems

q: A patient receiving vincristine reports new numbness and severe constipation. Which adverse-effect mechanism should be considered?
opts: A. Only renal crystal obstruction
B. A protective effect against neuropathy
C. Peripheral and autonomic neurotoxicity
D. An expected improvement in gut motility
exp: Vincristine can cause peripheral and autonomic neuropathy, including constipation or ileus; assess promptly.
opts_exp: A. Renal crystallization does not explain this characteristic symptom pair.
B. Vincristine is neurotoxic rather than protective against neuropathy.
C. Correct. Vincristine can cause peripheral and autonomic neuropathy, including constipation or ileus; assess promptly.
D. Vincristine can impair rather than improve gut motility.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 2: Oncology Supportive Care

q: Before a regimen with substantial tumor lysis risk, what laboratory pattern is important to anticipate?
opts: A. Permanent immunity to acute kidney injury
B. Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and secondary hypocalcemia
C. Isolated low uric acid with no other changes
D. Only hypernatremia
exp: Cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate, and purine precursors; hypocalcemia and AKI may follow.
opts_exp: A. Tumor lysis can cause acute kidney injury.
B. Correct. Cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate, and purine precursors; hypocalcemia and AKI may follow.
C. Low uric acid alone is not the characteristic untreated tumor lysis pattern.
D. Sodium elevation alone does not define tumor lysis syndrome.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 2: Oncology Supportive Care

q: Why should live vaccines be reviewed carefully before use during intensive cytotoxic chemotherapy?
opts: A. They may cause vaccine-associated infection in substantially immunocompromised patients
B. They are always more effective during neutropenia
C. They eliminate all infection risks
D. All vaccines contain replicating organisms
exp: Substantial immunosuppression can make live vaccines unsafe; assess vaccine type and timing with the oncology team.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Substantial immunosuppression can make live vaccines unsafe; assess vaccine type and timing with the oncology team.
B. Neutropenia is not a reason to assume enhanced vaccine safety or effectiveness.
C. No vaccine eliminates all infections.
D. Many vaccines are nonlive; recommendations depend on vaccine type and immune status.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 2: Oncology Supportive Care

q: Lactulose is titrated for hepatic encephalopathy. Which outcome most directly guides routine dose titration while avoiding dehydration?
opts: A. Profuse watery diarrhea at every dose
B. A serum lactulose concentration
C. Complete absence of bowel movements
D. An appropriate soft-stool frequency and clinical response
exp: Titrate to the prescribed soft-stool target and mental status; excessive diarrhea can cause volume and electrolyte loss.
opts_exp: A. Profuse diarrhea is an adverse effect rather than the goal.
B. Routine lactulose serum concentration monitoring is not used.
C. Absent bowel movements do not meet the intended titration target.
D. Correct. Titrate to the prescribed soft-stool target and mental status; excessive diarrhea can cause volume and electrolyte loss.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 4: Gastroenterology

q: A patient takes oral iron and a proton pump inhibitor. What potential absorption issue deserves review if iron response is poor?
opts: A. All oral iron is absorbed through the skin
B. Spacing by one minute reverses sustained acid suppression
C. Reduced gastric acidity may reduce absorption of some oral iron formulations
D. PPIs guarantee complete iron absorption
exp: Acid suppression can impair absorption of some iron formulations; evaluate adherence, formulation, bleeding, and other causes of poor response.
opts_exp: A. Oral iron is absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract.
B. Brief dose spacing does not remove the sustained pharmacodynamic effect of a PPI.
C. Correct. Acid suppression can impair absorption of some iron formulations; evaluate adherence, formulation, bleeding, and other causes of poor response.
D. Acid suppression does not guarantee effective iron absorption.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 4: Gastroenterology

q: Which mechanism explains why polyethylene glycol can treat constipation?
opts: A. Direct opioid receptor agonism
B. Osmotic retention of water in the intestinal lumen
C. Permanent inhibition of intestinal blood supply
D. Blocking all pancreatic enzyme release
exp: Polyethylene glycol is an osmotic laxative that retains water in stool.
opts_exp: A. Opioid agonism commonly causes constipation rather than treating it.
B. Correct. Polyethylene glycol is an osmotic laxative that retains water in stool.
C. Impaired blood supply is not a therapeutic laxative mechanism.
D. Pancreatic enzyme blockade is not its mechanism.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 4: Gastroenterology

q: An alert patient with diabetes has symptomatic hypoglycemia and can swallow safely. Which immediate approach is appropriate?
opts: A. Give rapid-acting oral carbohydrate and recheck glucose promptly
B. Give the usual prandial insulin first
C. Wait for the next scheduled meal
D. Use a high-fat meal as the fastest glucose source
exp: Rapid-acting carbohydrate treats an alert patient who can swallow; reassess glucose after approximately 15 minutes and repeat as needed.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Rapid-acting carbohydrate treats an alert patient who can swallow; reassess glucose after approximately 15 minutes and repeat as needed.
B. Insulin can worsen the hypoglycemia.
C. Symptomatic hypoglycemia requires prompt treatment.
D. Fat delays absorption and is not the fastest initial rescue carbohydrate.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 5: Endocrine & Metabolic

q: Which feature distinguishes basal insulin from mealtime insulin in a typical basal-bolus regimen?
opts: A. Basal insulin is only for immediate meal coverage
B. Basal insulin must always be withheld whenever a meal is missed
C. Basal insulin treats only post-meal glucose
D. Basal insulin supplies background insulin between meals and overnight
exp: Basal insulin supplies background requirements; prandial insulin addresses meal-related needs.
opts_exp: A. Rapid-acting mealtime insulin is designed for immediate meal coverage.
B. Especially in type 1 diabetes, basal insulin generally remains necessary despite fasting, with individualized dose adjustment.
C. Basal insulin addresses fasting and between-meal needs as well as overnight glucose.
D. Correct. Basal insulin supplies background requirements; prandial insulin addresses meal-related needs.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 5: Endocrine & Metabolic

q: Why must an SGLT2 inhibitor be considered in the differential when a patient has anion-gap acidosis and ketosis despite glucose below typical DKA values?
opts: A. They prevent all ketone production
B. They directly measure serum bicarbonate
C. These agents can be associated with euglycemic ketoacidosis
D. Normal-range glucose excludes every form of ketoacidosis
exp: SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis may occur without marked hyperglycemia; assess ketones, acid-base status, and precipitating factors urgently.
opts_exp: A. SGLT2 inhibitors do not prevent every episode of ketosis.
B. They are medications, not bicarbonate assays.
C. Correct. SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis may occur without marked hyperglycemia; assess ketones, acid-base status, and precipitating factors urgently.
D. Glucose alone cannot exclude euglycemic ketoacidosis.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 5: Endocrine & Metabolic

q: A serum creatinine value is rising rapidly during AKI. Why should an automatically reported eGFR be interpreted cautiously for dosing?
opts: A. A single eGFR determines all loading doses
B. Creatinine-based estimates generally assume a more stable creatinine state
C. The estimate directly measures every drug clearance
D. AKI eliminates all nonrenal clearance
exp: During changing renal function, creatinine-based equations may lag actual filtration; use trends, clinical context, and drug monitoring when available.
opts_exp: A. Loading doses depend substantially on distribution and target exposure, not only eGFR.
B. Correct. During changing renal function, creatinine-based equations may lag actual filtration; use trends, clinical context, and drug monitoring when available.
C. eGFR estimates filtration rather than directly measuring drug-specific clearance.
D. AKI does not eliminate all hepatic or other nonrenal clearance.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 6: Nephrology

q: A patient takes an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone. Which electrolyte especially requires monitoring?
opts: A. Potassium
B. Serum iron as the only test
C. Chloride only
D. No electrolyte monitoring is needed
exp: Both drugs can increase potassium, especially with impaired kidney function.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Both drugs can increase potassium, especially with impaired kidney function.
B. Iron testing does not replace potassium and renal-function monitoring.
C. Chloride alone does not detect the principal interaction risk.
D. Potassium and renal-function monitoring remain important.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 6: Nephrology

q: A patient is prescribed a phosphate binder for hyperphosphatemia in advanced CKD. When is administration generally most useful?
opts: A. Only during an overnight fast
B. Only after the binder has been stopped
C. Timing is unrelated to intestinal phosphate
D. With meals containing phosphate
exp: Binders act on dietary phosphate in the gut and are generally taken with meals; follow the specific product instructions.
opts_exp: A. Fasting administration misses the dietary phosphate load.
B. A stopped drug cannot bind intestinal phosphate.
C. Timing with food matters for phosphate binding.
D. Correct. Binders act on dietary phosphate in the gut and are generally taken with meals; follow the specific product instructions.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 6: Nephrology

q: An older adult has new confusion and urinary retention after starting diphenhydramine for sleep. Which medication effect is most relevant?
opts: A. A guaranteed bacterial infection
B. Vitamin replacement
C. Anticholinergic toxicity
D. Selective enhancement of cognition
exp: Diphenhydramine has substantial anticholinergic effects and can contribute to delirium and urinary retention.
opts_exp: A. An infection is possible clinically but is not established by this drug-related symptom pattern.
B. Diphenhydramine is not a vitamin replacement.
C. Correct. Diphenhydramine has substantial anticholinergic effects and can contribute to delirium and urinary retention.
D. It can impair rather than enhance cognition.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 7: Geriatrics

q: Which deprescribing approach is most appropriate for a long-term benzodiazepine when discontinuation is agreed upon?
opts: A. Double the dose first without a reason
B. Abruptly stop every patient immediately
C. Use an individualized gradual taper with monitoring
D. Replace it automatically with an anticholinergic sleep aid
exp: A gradual individualized taper reduces withdrawal risk and should include follow-up and non-drug support when appropriate.
opts_exp: A. Unnecessary dose escalation increases exposure and dependence.
B. Abrupt withdrawal can cause serious symptoms, including seizures.
C. Correct. A gradual individualized taper reduces withdrawal risk and should include follow-up and non-drug support when appropriate.
D. An anticholinergic sleep aid may add cognitive and fall risk.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 7: Geriatrics

q: An older adult has fallen repeatedly while taking several sedating medications. What is the most useful medication action?
opts: A. Review cumulative CNS effects and opportunities to reduce medication-related fall risk
B. Assume each drug is safe because it is prescribed
C. Add a sedative to prevent movement
D. Ignore recent dose changes
exp: Cumulative sedating effects, orthostasis, indications, and recent changes should be reviewed as part of a multifactorial falls assessment.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Cumulative sedating effects, orthostasis, indications, and recent changes should be reviewed as part of a multifactorial falls assessment.
B. Prescription status does not eliminate adverse effects.
C. Additional sedation can increase injury risk.
D. Dose changes can be important temporal clues.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 7: Geriatrics

q: A patient uses an inhaled corticosteroid. Which counseling point can reduce local adverse effects?
opts: A. Swallow every mouthful of rinse water
B. Use it only to reverse an acute attack immediately
C. Stop all inhaler technique review
D. Rinse the mouth and spit after use
exp: Rinsing and spitting after inhaled corticosteroid use helps reduce oral candidiasis; technique and spacer use when applicable also matter.
opts_exp: A. Spitting removes residual medication from the mouth.
B. An ICS alone is not an immediate bronchodilator rescue medication.
C. Technique remains central to effective inhaled therapy.
D. Correct. Rinsing and spitting after inhaled corticosteroid use helps reduce oral candidiasis; technique and spacer use when applicable also matter.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 8: Pulmonology & Vaccinations

q: Why is LABA monotherapy inappropriate in asthma?
opts: A. It provides permanent remission
B. Every LABA is an antibiotic
C. It does not provide the anti-inflammatory controller therapy required for safe asthma management
D. LABAs cannot bronchodilate
exp: Asthma treatment with a LABA requires accompanying ICS-containing therapy; bronchodilation alone does not address airway inflammation safely.
opts_exp: A. LABAs do not permanently cure asthma.
B. LABAs are beta2-agonists, not antibiotics.
C. Correct. Asthma treatment with a LABA requires accompanying ICS-containing therapy; bronchodilation alone does not address airway inflammation safely.
D. LABAs are bronchodilators.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 8: Pulmonology & Vaccinations

q: An adult has incomplete vaccine records. What should determine a catch-up plan?
opts: A. Assume one vaccine replaces all others
B. The current applicable schedule, documented doses, age, and risk conditions
C. Restart every vaccine series automatically
D. Use a childhood schedule without reviewing age
exp: Review current authoritative schedules and valid prior doses; incomplete records require an individualized catch-up assessment.
opts_exp: A. Vaccines target different pathogens and do not substitute universally.
B. Correct. Review current authoritative schedules and valid prior doses; incomplete records require an individualized catch-up assessment.
C. Most interrupted series do not automatically need restarting.
D. Adult recommendations depend on age and risk.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 8: Pulmonology & Vaccinations

q: A fictional dosing exercise specifies 12 mg/kg per dose for a child weighing 18 kg, below the stated maximum. What is the calculated dose?
opts: B. 216 mg
C. 1.5 mg
exp: 12 mg/kg/dose × 18 kg = 216 mg per dose; this is arithmetic practice, not a drug-specific recommendation.
opts_exp: A. This is tenfold below 12 × 18.
B. Correct. 12 mg/kg/dose × 18 kg = 216 mg per dose; this is arithmetic practice, not a drug-specific recommendation.
C. Dividing weight by dose rate does not produce the prescribed dose.
D. This is tenfold above the calculated dose.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 9: Pediatrics

q: A liquid contains 125 mg per 5 mL. A verified order is for 250 mg. What volume supplies that dose?
opts: A. 5 mL
B. 10 mL
C. 25 mL
D. 2.5 mL
opts_exp: A. 5 mL contains 125 mg.
B. Correct. 250 mg × 5 mL/125 mg = 10 mL.
C. 25 mL contains 625 mg.
D. 2.5 mL contains 62.5 mg.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 9: Pediatrics

q: Which instruction best reduces liquid-medication measurement errors at home?
opts: A. Alternate teaspoons and tablespoons freely
B. Estimate by the height of liquid in a cup
C. Measure in mL with an appropriate oral syringe
D. Use a household soup spoon
exp: Use mL-only instructions and an appropriately sized oral syringe; demonstrate the dose and check understanding.
opts_exp: A. Mixing units increases error risk.
B. Visual estimation is imprecise.
C. Correct. Use mL-only instructions and an appropriately sized oral syringe; demonstrate the dose and check understanding.
D. Household spoons vary in volume.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 9: Pediatrics

q: A new drug claim is based on a press release without a full publication. Which response best reflects evidence appraisal?
opts: A. Ignore the comparator and endpoint
B. Treat the headline as a complete efficacy and safety review
C. Seek full methods, population, outcomes, harms, and limitations before drawing a firm conclusion
D. Assume peer review has occurred
exp: Appraisal requires enough methodological and outcome detail to assess the claim and its limits.
opts_exp: A. Comparator and endpoint determine what a result actually means.
B. A press release omits details needed to judge validity and applicability.
C. Correct. Appraisal requires enough methodological and outcome detail to assess the claim and its limits.
D. A press release is not proof of peer review.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 12: Drug Information

q: A patient cannot explain a new anticoagulant plan after counseling. Which next step best uses teach-back?
opts: A. Ask the patient to describe how they will take it, then clarify gaps without blame
B. Ask only whether everything is clear
C. Repeat jargon more loudly
D. Assume silence proves comprehension
exp: Teach-back checks how well the explanation worked and provides a chance to clarify the plan.
opts_exp: A. Correct. Teach-back checks how well the explanation worked and provides a chance to clarify the plan.
B. A yes/no question can miss misunderstandings.
C. Volume and jargon do not establish understanding.
D. Silence does not demonstrate comprehension.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 12: Drug Information

q: Two guidelines disagree. Which comparison is most useful before applying either recommendation?
opts: A. Only the number of pages
B. Only the color of the logo
C. Which title is easier to remember
D. Publication date, population, evidence review, outcome priorities, and recommendation strength
exp: Differences in evidence, population, timing, and value judgments can explain divergent recommendations.
opts_exp: A. Length is not evidence quality.
B. Brand appearance does not establish applicability.
C. Memorability does not establish clinical validity.
D. Correct. Differences in evidence, population, timing, and value judgments can explain divergent recommendations.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 12: Drug Information

q: A fictional oral drug has bioavailability 0.5. If the required systemic dose is 100 mg, what oral dose gives that exposure under linear kinetics?
opts: A. 100 mg
B. 200 mg
C. 25 mg
D. 50 mg
exp: Oral dose = systemic dose/F = 100/0.5 = 200 mg.
opts_exp: A. 100 mg gives 50 mg systemically.
B. Correct. Oral dose = systemic dose/F = 100/0.5 = 200 mg.
C. 25 mg gives 12.5 mg systemically at F=0.5.
D. 50 mg gives 25 mg systemically.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 3: Pharmacokinetics

q: A fictional drug has Vd 40 L and clearance 4 L/hour. What is its approximate elimination half-life under a one-compartment model?
opts: A. 69.3 hours
B. 0.069 hours
C. 0.693 hours
D. 6.93 hours
opts_exp: A. This is tenfold above the calculated half-life.
B. This reverses the Vd/clearance relationship and scale.
C. This is tenfold below 0.693 × 40/4.
D. Correct. Half-life = 0.693 × Vd/CL = 0.693 × 40/4 = 6.93 hours.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 3: Pharmacokinetics

q: A diagnostic test detects 90 of 100 patients who truly have a disease. What is its sensitivity in this sample?
exp: Sensitivity = true positives/all with disease = 90/100 = 90%.
opts_exp: A. 10% is the false-negative proportion among diseased patients.
B. 50% does not follow from these counts.
C. Correct. Sensitivity = true positives/all with disease = 90/100 = 90%.
D. Ten diseased patients were missed, so sensitivity is not 100%.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 10: Biostatistics

q: Among 200 participants without disease, a test is negative in 180. What is specificity?
exp: Specificity = true negatives/all without disease = 180/200 = 90%.
opts_exp: A. 20 is the number of false positives, not the specificity percentage.
C. Correct. Specificity = true negatives/all without disease = 180/200 = 90%.
D. 10% is the false-positive proportion among nondiseased participants.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 10: Biostatistics

q: A treatment causes an adverse event in 8% of participants versus 3% with control over six months. What is the number needed to harm over six months?
exp: NNH = 1/(0.08 − 0.03) = 20 over the specified follow-up.
opts_exp: A. Correct. NNH = 1/(0.08 − 0.03) = 20 over the specified follow-up.
B. 33 approximates the inverse of the control risk rather than the risk increase.
C. 5 is the absolute risk increase in percentage points, not NNH.
D. Adding the event rates does not calculate NNH.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 10: Biostatistics

q: A fictional infusion order is 15 mL/hour for 8 hours. What total volume is delivered if it runs uninterrupted?
opts: A. 150 mL
C. 23 mL
D. 120 mL
exp: Volume = rate × time = 15 × 8 = 120 mL.
opts_exp: A. 150 mL would take 10 hours at this rate.
B. Dividing rate by time gives the wrong units.
C. Adding a rate to a duration is not valid.
D. Correct. Volume = rate × time = 15 × 8 = 120 mL.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 1, Ch 7: Fluids, Electrolytes & Nutrition

q: For a linear IV drug at steady state, the total daily dose is 600 mg and clearance is 3 L/hour. What is AUC over 24 hours?
opts: A. 50 mg·hour/L
B. 100 mg·hour/L
C. 200 mg·hour/L
D. 1800 mg·hour/L
exp: Steady-state AUC24 = total daily dose/CL = 600/3 = 200 mg·hour/L.
opts_exp: A. This is one quarter of dose/clearance.
B. This is half of dose/clearance.
C. Correct. Steady-state AUC24 = total daily dose/CL = 600/3 = 200 mg·hour/L.
D. Multiplying dose by clearance gives the wrong units.
ref: Original AinaDara practice item; ACCP 2024 study topic: Vol 2, Ch 3: Pharmacokinetics
